# Plain-Language Summary of Section 7

This section covers two related topics: (1) when each side promises to protect the other from outside lawsuits ("indemnification"), and (2) hard caps on how much money either side can be forced to pay if things go wrong ("limitation of liability").

## 7.1 Mutual Indemnification — Who pays if someone else sues?

Both sides make the same promise to each other. If a third party (someone outside this contract) sues one side because of something the OTHER side did wrong, the side that caused the problem has to step in, defend the lawsuit, and pay any resulting costs.

The promise kicks in for three kinds of problems:

- **(a) Broken promises in the contract** — if the responsible party violated something it promised in the agreement.
- **(b) Serious misconduct** — if the responsible party was grossly careless or acted intentionally badly.
- **(c) IP infringement** — if the product or work delivered (the "Deliverables") is accused of copying or stealing someone else's intellectual property (like a patent, copyright, or trade secret).

The IP promise (c) has three important **carve-outs** — situations where the provider is off the hook:

- (i) The customer modified the Deliverables themselves.
- (ii) The customer combined the Deliverables with something else, and it's only that combination that causes the infringement.
- (iii) The customer used the Deliverables in a way the contract didn't allow.

## 7.2 Indemnification Procedure — The rules for handling the lawsuit

If you're the side being sued and you want the other side to cover you, you have to:

- **(a)** Tell them about the lawsuit promptly, in writing. (If you're late, they only get out of their obligation to the extent that the delay actually hurt them.)
- **(b)** Hand over control of the defense and any settlement to them. BUT they can't settle in a way that admits you did something wrong, or forces you to do something (beyond paying money), without your written OK — and you can't unreasonably say no.
- **(c)** Cooperate reasonably with them, and they pay for your cooperation costs.

## 7.3 Limitation of Liability — Caps on the money at stake

This is written in all caps because courts generally require these clauses to be conspicuous to be enforceable. It has two parts:

**Part 1 — No "soft" damages.** Neither side can sue the other for indirect, ripple-effect harms like lost profits, lost revenue, lost data, or reputational damage — even if the harmed side warned the other that these losses might happen.

**Part 2 — A hard dollar cap.** The total amount either side can ever be forced to pay under this contract is capped at the LARGER of:

- (A) whatever the customer paid (or owed) the provider in the 12 months before the problem started, OR
- (B) $100,000.

**Big exceptions — the caps DON'T apply to:**

- (i) The indemnification promises in 7.1.
- (ii) Breaking the confidentiality rules in Section 9.
- (iii) Gross negligence or willful (intentional) misconduct.
- (iv) One party infringing the other's own IP.

For these four categories, there is no dollar limit and no exclusion of soft damages — the exposure is unlimited.

---

# Key Legal Terms in Plain Language

- **Indemnify / Indemnification** — A promise to cover someone else's costs and losses if they get hit with a legal problem caused by you. Think of it as "I've got your back financially."
- **Defend** — Actually take on running the lawsuit — hiring the lawyers, showing up in court — not just paying the bill afterward.
- **Hold harmless** — Make sure the other side ends up with no financial hit from the problem.
- **Indemnifying Party / Indemnified Party** — The one making the promise ("indemnifying") vs. the one receiving the protection ("indemnified").
- **Third-party claim** — A lawsuit or demand from someone outside the contract (not you, not your counterparty).
- **Representation, warranty, or covenant** — Statements or promises in the contract. A *representation* is a statement of fact ("we own this code"). A *warranty* is a guarantee about a fact. A *covenant* is a promise to do or not do something.
- **Gross negligence** — Much worse than an ordinary mistake — a serious, reckless disregard for the consequences.
- **Willful misconduct** — Intentional bad behavior — doing something wrong on purpose.
- **Infringe / Misappropriate** — To use someone else's intellectual property without permission (infringement typically for patents/copyrights/trademarks; misappropriation typically for trade secrets).
- **Deliverables** — The work products the provider hands over under the contract (software, reports, designs, etc.).
- **Tender control of the defense** — Formally hand the lawsuit over to the other side so they run it.
- **Settlement** — An agreement to end a lawsuit, usually by paying money, without a court ruling.
- **Materially prejudiced** — Meaningfully hurt or disadvantaged. Small annoyances don't count.
- **Indirect / Incidental / Consequential damages** — Downstream ripple-effect losses (like lost future profits) as opposed to "direct" damages, which are the immediate cost of the problem itself.
- **Special damages** — Unusual losses specific to the harmed party's situation.
- **Punitive / Exemplary damages** — Extra money awarded to punish especially bad behavior, over and above making the victim whole.
- **Under any theory of liability** — No matter what legal argument someone uses (contract, negligence, statute, etc.), the rule still applies.
- **Cumulative liability** — The running total of everything owed under this contract, not a per-incident cap.
- **Cap / Liability cap** — The maximum amount either side can be forced to pay.
- **Carve-out** — An exception that pulls a specific situation out of a general rule.

---

# The Bottom Line

- Both sides protect each other from outside lawsuits caused by their own broken promises, serious misconduct, or IP problems — with standard exceptions when the customer misuses or modifies what was delivered.
- If one side is sued, the other takes over the defense, but can't admit fault or impose obligations on the sued side without permission.
- Neither side can collect "soft" damages like lost profits, and total damages are capped at the greater of one year of fees or $100,000 — EXCEPT for the four carve-outs (indemnity, confidentiality, gross negligence/willful misconduct, and IP infringement), where liability is uncapped.

## Plain-Language Summary

This section covers two things: who pays if something goes wrong, and how much they could ever have to pay.

**Who covers what (Section 7.1 - Indemnification)**
If one company's actions cause a lawsuit or claim from someone outside the contract (a "third party"), that company has to step in, cover the legal costs, and pay any resulting damages - for the other company. This applies in three situations:
- One side broke a promise it made in the contract.
- One side acted recklessly or intentionally caused harm.
- One side's deliverables (software, work product, etc.) are accused of stealing or infringing someone else's patent, copyright, or other intellectual property.

That third protection has limits, though. If the company receiving the deliverables modified them, mixed them with other outside material that caused the problem, or used them in a way the contract didn't allow, the company that built the deliverables isn't on the hook for that IP claim.

**How a claim gets handled (Section 7.2 - Procedure)**
If you're the one being protected and someone sues you, you need to:
- Tell the other company about it promptly (if you're late, they can still refuse to help you if the delay actually hurt their ability to defend the case).
- Let them take over the legal defense and settlement decisions - though they can't agree to a settlement that admits fault or forces you to do something (besides pay money) without your sign-off.
- Cooperate reasonably, with them covering your costs for doing so.

**Caps on damages (Section 7.3 - Limitation of Liability)**
This part limits how much money either company could ever owe the other, with some carve-outs where the limits don't apply.

The carve-outs (no cap applies here):
- The indemnification promises above.
- Breaking confidentiality rules.
- Reckless or intentional misconduct.
- Stealing or infringing the other company's intellectual property.

For everything else, two protections kick in:
1. Neither company can be sued for indirect or knock-on damages - things like lost profits, lost business, reputational harm, or lost data - even if they knew those losses were possible.
2. Total liability for anything else is capped at whichever is higher: the fees paid in the prior 12 months, or $100,000.

## Key Legal Terms Defined

- **Indemnify / Indemnification**: A promise to cover someone else's losses or legal costs if a specific bad thing happens. Think of it as one party agreeing to "foot the bill" for the other in defined situations.

- **Hold harmless**: Similar to indemnify - a promise not to let the other party suffer financial harm from a covered claim.

- **Third-party claim**: A lawsuit or legal demand brought by someone outside the contract (not one company suing the other, but an outsider suing one of them).

- **Gross negligence**: Carelessness so extreme it goes far beyond an honest mistake - a serious, obvious failure to use reasonable care.

- **Willful misconduct**: Doing something harmful on purpose, or with reckless disregard for the consequences.

- **Deliverables**: The product, software, or work being provided under the contract.

- **Infringe / misappropriate (intellectual property)**: Using or copying someone's patented invention, copyrighted work, trademark, or trade secret without permission.

- **Tender control of the defense**: Hand over the responsibility (and decision-making power) for defending against a lawsuit to the other party.

- **Consequential / indirect damages**: Losses that aren't the direct, immediate result of a problem but ripple outward from it - like lost future profits or damage to reputation, as opposed to the direct cost of fixing the problem itself.

- **Punitive / exemplary damages**: Extra damages a court awards to punish especially bad behavior, beyond just compensating for the actual loss.

- **Liability cap**: A dollar ceiling on how much one party can ever be required to pay the other, no matter how large the actual damages turn out to be.

## Bottom Line

Each company promises to clean up messes it directly causes (broken promises, reckless behavior, or IP theft), following a defined process for handling claims. But outside of those specific situations, neither company can be on the hook for indirect losses like lost profits, and their total liability is generally capped at either last year's fees or $100,000, whichever is bigger.

# Section 7 in Plain Language

## What this section does

Section 7 answers two questions: who pays when an outsider sues one of the parties because of something the other party did, and how much either party can be on the hook for if things go wrong between them. It is a two-way clause. The same rules apply whether you are the Customer or the Provider.

## 7.1 — Mutual Indemnification: who covers whom, and for what

If a third party (someone who is not a party to this contract) brings a claim against you, and that claim traces back to the other party's conduct, the other party has to step in, run the defense, and pay the resulting costs. This covers three situations:

1. **They broke a promise in the contract.** If the other party breached a representation, warranty, or covenant and that breach leads to an outside claim against you, they cover it.
2. **They were seriously careless or acted deliberately.** Ordinary mistakes are not enough. This applies only to gross negligence or willful misconduct.
3. **Their deliverables infringe someone's intellectual property.** If a third party alleges that what the other party delivered violates a patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret, the delivering party covers the claim, as long as you were using the deliverables the way the contract allows.

The IP protection in item 3 has three carve-outs. The other party does not have to cover you if the infringement happened because:

- you modified the deliverables yourself,
- you combined them with something they did not supply, and the infringement would not have happened without that combination, or
- you used them in a way the contract does not permit.

What gets covered is broad: the costs of the claim itself plus any resulting losses, damages, settlements, judgments, fines, penalties, and reasonable fees for outside lawyers.

## 7.2 — Indemnification Procedure: how to trigger the protection

To get the benefit of 7.1, the party being protected has to do three things:

1. **Notify the other side promptly and in writing.** If you are slow to notify, you do not automatically lose coverage. You only lose it to the extent the delay actually hurt the other party's ability to defend the claim.
2. **Hand over control of the defense and any settlement.** The indemnifying party gets to pick the strategy and the lawyers. One limit: they cannot agree to a settlement that admits you were liable or forces you to do (or stop doing) something without your written consent, and you cannot refuse consent unreasonably.
3. **Cooperate reasonably**, with the indemnifying party paying for your time and expenses in doing so.

## 7.3 — Limitation of Liability: the cap on what either side can owe

This paragraph is in capital letters because courts in many jurisdictions require limitation clauses to be conspicuous. It has two parts.

**Part one: no indirect damages.** Neither party can recover from the other for indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages, nor for lost profits, lost revenue, loss of goodwill, or loss of data. This applies no matter how the damage happened or what legal theory is used, and even if the party was warned in advance that such damage was possible.

**Part two: a dollar cap on everything else.** Each party's total liability under the contract, added up over the whole relationship, is limited to whichever is larger:

- (A) the fees the Customer paid or owed the Provider in the twelve months before the first event that caused the liability, or
- (B) $100,000.

**Four things sit outside both limits.** The damages exclusion and the dollar cap do not apply to:

1. indemnification obligations under 7.1,
2. breaches of the confidentiality section (Section 9),
3. gross negligence or willful misconduct, and
4. one party infringing the other party's intellectual property.

For those four categories, liability is uncapped and can include the indirect damages otherwise excluded.

## Practical takeaways

- Both parties are protected against third-party claims caused by the other's contract breaches, serious misconduct, or infringing deliverables.
- The party being protected has to act quickly, hand over the defense, and cooperate, or risk losing some of the protection.
- For disputes directly between the parties, recoverable damages are limited to direct losses and capped at the greater of twelve months of fees or $100,000.
- The cap disappears for indemnification, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence, willful misconduct, and IP infringement between the parties. Those are the areas of real exposure.

## Key terms defined

**Indemnify / Indemnification.** To compensate someone for a loss or cover their costs. In a contract, an indemnification clause shifts financial responsibility for certain claims from one party to the other.

**Hold harmless.** A promise not to hold the other party responsible for specified losses. It usually travels with "indemnify" and reinforces the same idea: you will not be left holding the bill.

**Defend.** In this context, an obligation to take over and pay for the legal defense of a claim, including hiring lawyers, rather than just reimbursing costs afterward.

**Indemnifying Party.** The party that has to pay and defend.

**Indemnified Parties.** The party being protected, along with its officers, directors, employees, and agents.

**Third-party claim.** A demand or lawsuit brought by someone who is not a party to this contract, such as a customer, a competitor, or a government agency.

**Claims.** The defined term for the demands, lawsuits, and legal proceedings themselves.

**Losses.** The defined term for the money that comes out of a Claim: damages, settlements, judgments, fines, penalties, costs, and reasonable outside lawyer fees.

**Representation.** A statement of fact one party makes to the other at signing (for example, "we own the software we are licensing to you").

**Warranty.** A promise that something is or will be true, such as a promise that the deliverables will work as described.

**Covenant.** A promise to do or not do something during the life of the contract.

**Breach.** Failing to keep a representation, warranty, or covenant.

**Gross negligence.** Extreme carelessness, well beyond an ordinary mistake. It implies a reckless disregard for obvious risks.

**Willful misconduct.** Intentional wrongdoing, or acting with knowledge that the conduct is wrong or harmful.

**Intellectual property (IP) rights.** Legal rights in creations of the mind, including patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets.

**Infringe.** To use someone's intellectual property without permission in a way the law prohibits.

**Misappropriate.** To take or use something improperly. In the IP context, it typically refers to trade secrets obtained or used without authorization.

**Deliverables.** The work product, software, documents, or other items one party provides to the other under the contract.

**Materially prejudiced.** Actually and significantly harmed. A delay in notification only matters if it made a real difference to the ability to defend the claim.

**Tender control of the defense.** To hand over decision-making authority for the lawsuit to the other party.

**Consent not to be unreasonably withheld.** You have a right to say no, but you must have a legitimate reason. You cannot refuse just to be difficult.

**Limitation of liability.** A clause that caps how much one party can owe the other, and rules out certain types of damages entirely.

**Direct damages.** Losses that flow immediately and naturally from a breach, such as the cost of fixing or replacing what was promised. These remain recoverable under 7.3, subject to the cap.

**Indirect / consequential damages.** Losses that result from the breach but only through a chain of events, such as a customer you lost because the software was down. Excluded under 7.3.

**Incidental damages.** Smaller costs incurred while dealing with a breach, such as expenses to find a replacement supplier. Excluded under 7.3.

**Special damages.** Losses unique to the injured party's particular circumstances that the breaching party may not have anticipated. Excluded under 7.3.

**Punitive / exemplary damages.** Money awarded to punish a wrongdoer rather than to compensate the victim. Excluded under 7.3.

**Lost profits, lost revenue, loss of goodwill, loss of data.** Specific categories of business harm listed to make clear they are excluded, regardless of whether a court would otherwise classify them as direct or indirect.

**Theory of liability.** The legal basis for a claim, such as breach of contract, negligence, or strict liability. The exclusion applies no matter which theory is used.

**Total cumulative liability.** The combined amount owed across all claims over the life of the contract, not a per-incident limit.

**Fees paid or payable.** Money actually paid plus money owed but not yet paid.

**Carve-out.** An exception to a general rule. Section 7.3 carves four categories out of the liability limits.

*This summary is for general understanding only and is not legal advice. Consult a lawyer before relying on any interpretation of contract terms.*

**Plain-English summary:** This section says each side must protect the other if its own actions cause certain outside claims. If one side breaks the agreement, acts recklessly on a serious level, intentionally does something wrong, or supplies work that allegedly violates someone else’s intellectual property rights, that side must handle the claim and cover the resulting costs. But that IP protection does **not** apply if the other side changed the work, combined it with other things that caused the problem, or used it in a way the contract did not allow.

It also explains **how** that process works: the protected side must promptly give written notice, let the other side control the defense and settlement, and cooperate reasonably. The defending side usually cannot settle in a way that admits fault for the other side or forces the other side to do something non-monetary without written consent.

On liability, the contract blocks most claims for **indirect or hard-to-measure damages** like lost profits, lost revenue, lost goodwill, or lost data. It also caps most direct liability at the greater of **(1) the amount paid or payable in the previous 12 months** or **(2) $100,000**. But that cap and damages exclusion do **not** apply to certain serious issues: indemnification duties, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence or willful misconduct, and infringement of the other party’s intellectual property rights.

**Key terms in plain language:**

| Term | Plain-language meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Pay for losses or claims that the other side suffers because of your conduct. |
| **Defend** | Take over and manage the legal defense of a claim. |
| **Hold harmless** | Protect the other side from having to bear the cost or burden of the claim. |
| **Indemnifying Party** | The side that must step in, defend, and pay when covered claims happen. |
| **Indemnified Parties** | The side being protected, plus its people like officers, employees, and agents. |
| **Third-party claim** | A claim brought by someone outside the contract, not by one of the two contracting parties themselves. |
| **Representation / warranty / covenant** | A statement of fact, a promise that something is true or will meet a standard, or a promise to do or not do something under the contract. |
| **Gross negligence** | Very serious carelessness, beyond ordinary mistakes. |
| **Willful misconduct** | Intentional wrongdoing or knowingly improper behavior. |
| **Deliverables** | The goods, work product, services, or materials one side provides under the agreement. |
| **Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property** | Violate someone else’s legal rights in things like software, inventions, trademarks, or confidential know-how. |
| **Scope expressly permitted** | The specific uses the contract clearly allows. |
| **Promptly notify in writing** | Give written notice without unreasonable delay. |
| **Sole control of the defense and settlement** | One side gets to run the legal strategy and settlement talks. |
| **Non-monetary obligation** | A duty other than paying money, like changing conduct, giving an admission, or taking a specific action. |
| **Prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld** | Approval must be in writing, and the other side cannot refuse unfairly. |
| **Materially prejudiced** | Seriously harmed in a practical way by the delay or failure. |
| **Indirect / consequential / special / punitive damages** | Extra categories of damages that go beyond the immediate direct loss, including knock-on business harm or punishment-style awards. |
| **Lost goodwill** | Damage to reputation, customer trust, or business relationships. |
| **Total cumulative liability** | The maximum total amount one side can owe under the agreement for covered claims. |

**Bottom line:** each side is responsible for serious problems it causes, but for most other disputes the contract sharply limits what either side can recover.

---

### 7.1 — Who covers whom

The protection runs **both ways**. If one side causes a problem, that side pays for the other side's legal mess — including the other side's officers, employees, and agents.

It's triggered by three things:
- **Breaking a promise** made in the contract
- **Gross negligence or willful misconduct** — reckless or deliberate bad behavior, not ordinary mistakes
- **IP infringement claims** — someone claims the Deliverables steal their intellectual property

The IP protection has **three escape hatches**. The provider is off the hook if you:
1. Modified the Deliverables yourself
2. Combined them with something they didn't supply, and that combination caused the problem
3. Used them in a way the contract doesn't allow

Practical takeaway: modify or mix in third-party material at your own risk.

### 7.2 — The procedure you must follow

To actually get covered, the protected side has to:
- **Tell the other side promptly, in writing.** Being late only hurts you if the delay actually damaged their ability to defend.
- **Hand over the defense entirely.** They pick the lawyers and decide on settlement — with one guardrail: they can't settle in a way that admits you did something wrong, or forces you to *do* something (not just pay money), without your OK.
- **Cooperate** — but they pay your costs for doing so.

### 7.3 — The money cap

Two separate limits, both in all-caps because courts often require that for enforceability.

**Limit 1:** Neither side pays for *indirect* damages — lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, lost data. Even if they were warned it could happen.

**Limit 2:** Total liability is capped at the **greater of** 12 months of fees paid, or **$100,000**. The $100,000 floor matters most in small contracts — if you only paid $20,000 in fees, you can still recover up to $100,000.

**Both limits have four exceptions** where liability is unlimited:
- Indemnification obligations under 7.1
- Confidentiality breaches (Section 9)
- Gross negligence or willful misconduct
- Infringing the other party's IP

---

### Key terms in plain language

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Pay for someone else's losses when a third party comes after them |
| **Defend** | Hire and pay the lawyers, not just reimburse afterward |
| **Hold harmless** | Make sure they walk away with no financial hit |
| **Third-party claim** | A lawsuit or demand from someone *outside* the contract — this whole section doesn't cover you suing each other |
| **Representation / warranty / covenant** | Statements of fact and promises made in the contract. Breaking one is a breach. |
| **Gross negligence** | Far worse than a normal mistake — reckless disregard |
| **Willful misconduct** | Doing something harmful on purpose |
| **Misappropriate** | Improperly taking or using someone's trade secrets |
| **Materially prejudiced** | Real, meaningful harm — a technicality doesn't count |
| **Tender sole control** | Fully hand over the driver's seat on the lawsuit |
| **Not unreasonably withheld** | You can't refuse consent just to be difficult |
| **Indirect / consequential damages** | Ripple-effect losses, not the direct harm itself |
| **Punitive / exemplary damages** | Money meant to punish, beyond covering actual losses |
| **Total cumulative liability** | Everything added together across the life of the contract — not per incident |

### Two things worth flagging to a lawyer

1. **The cap language is asymmetric.** It says "fees paid by Customer to Provider," so the fee-based prong tracks what *you* paid — but it caps *both* parties. Worth confirming that's intended.
2. **The exceptions swallow a lot of the cap.** Indemnification, confidentiality, gross negligence, and IP are carved out entirely — which is common, but it means the $100K/12-month ceiling applies to a narrower set of disputes than it first appears.

7.2 **Indemnification Procedure.** The Indemnified Parties shall (a) promptly
notify the Indemnifying Party in writing of any Claim (provided that failure to

the extent it is materially prejudiced thereby), (b) tender sole control of the
defense and settlement of the Claim to the Indemnifying Party (provided that

imposes any non-monetary obligation on, the Indemnified Parties without their
prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld), and (c) provide
reasonable cooperation at the Indemnifying Party's expense.

7.3 **Limitation of Liability.** EXCEPT FOR (i) A PARTY'S INDEMNIFICATION
OBLIGATIONS UNDER SECTION 7.1, (ii) BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY UNDER SECTION
9, (iii) A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, OR (iv) A PARTY'S
INFRINGEMENT OF THE OTHER PARTY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, IN NO EVENT
SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL,
CONSEQUENTIAL, SPECIAL, PUNITIVE, OR EXEMPLARY DAMAGES, OR FOR ANY LOST
PROFITS, LOST REVENUE, LOSS OF GOODWILL, OR LOSS OF DATA, HOWEVER CAUSED AND
UNDER ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH
DAMAGES. SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE LIABILITY
ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL NOT EXCEED THE GREATER OF
(A) THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER TO PROVIDER UNDER THIS AGREEMENT IN
THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS PRECEDING THE FIRST EVENT GIVING RISE TO LIABILITY, OR
(B) ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND U.S. DOLLARS ($100,000).

## Plain-language summary

**Section 7 covers who pays when something goes wrong, and caps how much either side can owe.**

**7.1: Each side protects the other from outside lawsuits.** If a third party sues one company because of the other company's actions, the company at fault covers the legal costs and any resulting payouts. This applies when the at-fault party:
- broke a promise or guarantee in the contract,
- was grossly negligent or acted intentionally wrong, or
- delivered work that infringes someone else's intellectual property (IP), such as a patent, copyright, or trademark.

The IP protection has exceptions. It doesn't apply if the other party changed the deliverable, combined it with third-party materials that caused the problem, or used it in a way the contract doesn't allow.

**7.2: How a claim must be handled.** The protected party must:
- tell the other side in writing promptly (a delay only matters if it actually hurts the other side's defense),
- let the other side run the defense and settlement, and
- cooperate, at the other side's expense.

The defending party can't settle in a way that admits fault for the protected party, or forces them to do or stop doing something, without their written consent. That consent can't be unreasonably refused.

**7.3: Limits on what each side can owe.**
- Neither side owes the other for indirect or "knock-on" losses. This includes lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, and lost data.
- Total liability is capped at the **greater of** (a) the fees paid or owed in the 12 months before the first problem, or (b) **$100,000**.
- **Exceptions with no cap and no knock-on-loss protection:**
  - indemnification duties under 7.1,
  - breaches of confidentiality (Section 9),
  - gross negligence or intentional misconduct, and
  - infringing the other party's IP.

## Key terms

- **Indemnify / hold harmless:** Pay for another party's losses and legal costs so they aren't left bearing them.
- **Indemnifying Party:** The side who has to cover the costs. Here, both sides can be in this role.
- **Indemnified Parties:** The protected side, including its officers, directors, employees, and agents.
- **Claim:** A lawsuit, demand, or legal proceeding brought by an outsider (a third party).
- **Losses:** Money owed because of a claim, including damages, settlements, fines, and reasonable outside lawyer fees.
- **Representation, warranty, covenant:** Statements of fact, guarantees, and promises made in the contract.
- **Gross negligence:** Extreme carelessness, well beyond an ordinary mistake.
- **Willful misconduct:** Deliberately doing something wrong.
- **Deliverables:** The products or work the provider hands over under the contract.
- **Infringe / misappropriate:** Use someone else's IP without permission, or take it improperly.
- **Tender control:** Hand over the running of the defense and settlement.
- **Prejudiced:** Harmed. Late notice only matters if it damages the defense.
- **Indirect, incidental, consequential, special damages:** Losses that flow indirectly from a problem rather than directly from it, such as a lost deal caused by a delayed product.
- **Punitive / exemplary damages:** Extra money meant to punish, not to compensate.
- **Goodwill:** The value of a company's reputation and customer relationships.
- **Cumulative liability cap:** The maximum total a party can owe across all claims combined.

## Worth noting

- The cap is a floor of $100,000, so it protects a party in a small contract but may be far above the fees paid.
- Because indemnification is excluded from the cap, third-party IP claims could produce very large, uncapped exposure for either side.

This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Have a lawyer review before signing.

## What Section 7 Actually Requires

- **Each side has to defend and pay for the other** when an outside person or company sues the other side because of something the first side did wrong — specifically, breaking a promise in the contract, being extremely careless or acting on purpose to cause harm, or delivering something that steals or copies someone else's intellectual property.

- **The IP-infringement protection has three carve-outs.** You are NOT protected if the problem was caused by (i) changes you made to what was delivered, (ii) combining what was delivered with other stuff that wasn't supplied by the other party (and the problem only happened because of that mix), or (iii) using what was delivered in a way the contract doesn't allow.

- **If you get sued, you must (a) tell the other party in writing right away, (b) hand them the steering wheel to defend and settle the case, and (c) cooperate reasonably (they pay your out-of-pocket costs for helping).** If you're late to notify them, they can only reduce their obligation to the extent the delay actually hurt their ability to defend — not use it as a free pass.

- **The party running the defense cannot settle in a way that admits you did something wrong or forces you to do something (like stop selling a product) without your written OK** — and you can't unreasonably say no.

- **Neither side can be sued for "soft" damages** like lost profits, lost revenue, lost future business, reputation damage, or lost data — even if the other side warned them these losses could happen.

- **There is a hard dollar cap on total liability**: whichever is BIGGER of (A) the fees the customer paid or owed the provider in the 12 months before the problem started, or (B) $100,000.

- **Four things break through both the "no soft damages" rule AND the dollar cap** — meaning unlimited exposure: (1) the indemnification promises in 7.1, (2) breaking the confidentiality section (Section 9), (3) gross negligence or willful misconduct, and (4) infringing the other party's IP.

- **Bottom line for you as the business owner**: for ordinary mistakes and disputes, your worst-case bill is the 12-month fees or $100k (whichever is greater). But if you seriously mess up (grossly negligent, deliberate wrongdoing, leaking their secrets, stealing their IP, or triggering an indemnity claim), the cap disappears and you're exposed to the full amount.

## Key Terms Glossary

- **Indemnify / hold harmless** — A promise to step in and pay for the other side's legal problems (defense costs, settlements, judgments) so they don't end up out of pocket.

- **Third-party claim** — A lawsuit, demand, or legal action brought by someone who is NOT you and NOT the other party to the contract (like a customer, competitor, or regulator suing one of you).

- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct** — Gross negligence is being so careless it goes way beyond a normal mistake (reckless disregard); willful misconduct is knowing what you're doing is wrong and doing it anyway on purpose.

- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation** — Using, copying, or delivering something that violates someone else's patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret rights without permission.

- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages** — "Ripple effect" losses (like lost profits from a shutdown), side costs tied to the main problem (like renting a replacement), and extra punishment money a court adds to make an example of the wrongdoer — all beyond the direct, obvious cost of the harm itself.

- **Cap on liability** — A pre-agreed ceiling on the maximum dollar amount one side can ever be forced to pay the other, no matter how bad the damage gets.

- **Sole control of the defense** — The indemnifying party gets to fully run the lawsuit — pick the lawyers, decide the strategy, and negotiate the settlement — instead of the party being sued.

- **Materially prejudiced** — Meaningfully hurt in a real, significant way (not just a minor inconvenience) — here, it means the late notice actually damaged the defender's ability to fight the case.

- **Four things escape both the cap and the indirect-damages exclusion:** (i) the indemnification duties in 7.1, (ii) breaches of the confidentiality section (Section 9), (iii) gross negligence or willful misconduct, and (iv) one side infringing the other side's intellectual property. For those, there is no dollar ceiling and the full range of damages is available.

## Key terms

- **Indemnify / hold harmless:** One side promises to pay the other side's losses and legal costs if a particular kind of problem comes up, so the protected side does not end up out of pocket.

- **Third-party claim:** A lawsuit, demand, or complaint brought by someone outside the contract (a customer, a competitor, a regulator), not a dispute between the two signing companies themselves.

- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct:** Gross negligence is carelessness so extreme it goes far beyond an ordinary mistake; willful misconduct is doing something wrong on purpose or knowing it will cause harm.

- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation:** Using someone else's protected creation (their patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret) without permission, whether by copying it, building on it, or taking it improperly.

- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages:** Consequential damages are downstream losses caused by a problem (like lost sales); incidental damages are the smaller side costs of dealing with it (like paying to find a replacement); punitive damages are extra money a court adds to punish bad behavior rather than to cover an actual loss.

- **Cap on liability:** The maximum dollar amount one side can ever be required to pay the other under the contract, regardless of how big the actual loss was.

- **Sole control of the defense:** The side paying for the lawsuit gets to pick the lawyers, run the strategy, and decide whether and how to settle, without the other side second-guessing those decisions.

- **Materially prejudiced:** Genuinely harmed in a way that matters, for example, a late notice that cost the defending side a real chance to win or settle cheaply, rather than a technical slip that changed nothing.

# Section 7 — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

7.1 **Mutual Indemnification.** Each Party (the "Indemnifying Party") shall
defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the other Party and its officers,
directors, employees, and agents (the "Indemnified Parties") from and against
any and all third-party claims, demands, actions, suits, or proceedings

Indemnifying Party's Deliverables, when used in accordance with this Agreement,
infringe or misappropriate any third party's intellectual property rights,
provided that the foregoing (c) shall not apply to the extent a Claim arises
from (i) modifications made by the Indemnified Parties, (ii) combination of the
Deliverables with materials not supplied by the Indemnifying Party where the
infringement would not have occurred but for such combination, or (iii) use of
the Deliverables outside the scope expressly permitted under this Agreement.

7.2 **Indemnification Procedure.** The Indemnified Parties shall (a) promptly
notify the Indemnifying Party in writing of any Claim (provided that failure to

7.3 **Limitation of Liability.** EXCEPT FOR (i) A PARTY'S INDEMNIFICATION
OBLIGATIONS UNDER SECTION 7.1, (ii) BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY UNDER SECTION
9, (iii) A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, OR (iv) A PARTY'S
INFRINGEMENT OF THE OTHER PARTY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, IN NO EVENT
SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL,
CONSEQUENTIAL, SPECIAL, PUNITIVE, OR EXEMPLARY DAMAGES, OR FOR ANY LOST
PROFITS, LOST REVENUE, LOSS OF GOODWILL, OR LOSS OF DATA, HOWEVER CAUSED AND
UNDER ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH
DAMAGES. SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE LIABILITY
ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL NOT EXCEED THE GREATER OF
(A) THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER TO PROVIDER UNDER THIS AGREEMENT IN

- **Both sides owe protection to the other** if an outside person or company makes a claim because that side broke the contract, made a serious mistake, acted intentionally wrong, or provided work/product that allegedly violates someone else’s IP rights.
- **That protection means three things:** the responsible side must handle the defense, pay the losses, and protect the other side and its people from the cost of the claim.
- **IP-infringement protection only applies in a limited situation:** it covers claims that the provider’s deliverables, used as the contract allows, violate someone else’s IP rights.
- **That IP promise does not apply** if the other side changed the deliverables, combined them with something the provider did not supply and that combination caused the problem, or used them in a way the contract did not allow.
- **If a claim comes up, the protected side must act quickly:** give written notice promptly, let the other side control the defense and settlement, and reasonably help as needed.
- **Late notice does not automatically cancel coverage:** the paying/defending side is excused only if the delay actually hurt its ability to defend the claim in an important way.
- **The defending side controls the case, but with limits:** it cannot settle in a way that admits the other side did something wrong or forces the other side to do something other than pay money, unless the other side agrees in writing.
- **Liability is capped in most cases:** each side’s total liability is limited to the greater of **(a) fees paid or payable in the 12 months before the first event that caused liability** or **(b) $100,000**. But that cap, and the ban on indirect/consequential/punitive-type damages, **do not apply** to: **indemnity obligations under 7.1, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence or willful misconduct, or one party infringing the other party’s IP rights**.

**Key terms**

- **Indemnify / hold harmless:** to cover the other side’s costs and losses so they do not have to bear them themselves.
- **Third-party claim:** a claim brought by someone outside the contract, such as a customer, vendor, competitor, or rights holder.
- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct:** gross negligence is an extreme lack of care; willful misconduct is doing something wrong on purpose.
- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation:** using or copying someone else’s protected idea, code, content, invention, trademark, or trade secret without the right to do so.
- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages:** extra kinds of damages beyond direct loss, such as knock-on business harm, side costs caused by the problem, or money meant to punish.
- **Cap on liability:** the maximum amount one side can be made to pay under the contract.
- **Sole control of the defense:** one side gets to choose the lawyers and make the main decisions about how to fight or settle the claim.
- **Materially prejudiced:** meaningfully harmed in a practical way, such as losing a real chance to defend the case well because notice came too late.

## What Section 7 actually requires

- **Each side agrees to cover the other's outside-lawsuit problems it caused.** If someone outside this contract (a customer, vendor, regulator, etc.) sues you because of *my* broken promise, *my* recklessness/bad faith, or because *my* deliverables copied someone's IP — I pay the lawyers, the settlement, and the judgment. Same rule in reverse. It's mutual and symmetrical.

- **Only outside claims count.** This section does nothing for disputes between the two of you. If you're just unhappy with each other, that's ordinary breach-of-contract territory, not this.

- **The IP promise has three big holes.** I don't owe you IP protection if you *changed* my deliverables, if you *combined* them with something I didn't supply and that combination caused the problem, or if you used them *outside* what the contract allows. Practical takeaway: modify or mix my work and you may be on your own.

- **You must report a claim fast and hand over the wheel.** Notify in writing promptly, then let the other side run the defense and settlement. Late notice doesn't automatically kill your protection — only to the extent the delay actually hurt their ability to defend.

- **One guardrail on handing over the wheel:** they can't sign a settlement that admits you did something wrong, or that forces you to *do* something (recall a product, stop using software, apologize publicly), without your written OK. You must cooperate, but they pay your costs of cooperating.

- **Neither side can be sued for ripple-effect losses** — lost profits, lost revenue, lost data, damaged reputation. Even if the loss was foreseeable and warned about. This is often the biggest number in a real dispute, and both sides give it up.

- **The money cap: the greater of (a) fees paid/payable in the 12 months before the first triggering event, or (b) $100,000.** So $100,000 is the floor — the cap never drops below it even on a small contract. On a big contract the cap floats up with your spend.

- **Four things escape the ripple-damages ban:** indemnification duties (7.1), confidentiality breaches (Section 9), gross negligence or willful misconduct, and infringing the *other party's* IP. ⚠️ Two things to press your lawyer on: (1) the drafting is ambiguous about whether those four exceptions also break the dollar cap, or only the ripple-damages ban — "SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING" can be read either way, and it matters enormously; (2) the cap is measured by *fees you pay the Provider*, which sets the ceiling on the Provider's exposure to you and on yours to them using the same number.

---

## Key terms

- **Indemnify / hold harmless** — I agree to pay your costs and shield your wallet when a problem I caused lands on you.

- **Third-party claim** — a complaint, demand, or lawsuit from someone who isn't one of the two signers of this contract.

- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct** — gross negligence is being *extremely* careless, well past an ordinary mistake; willful misconduct is doing the harmful thing on purpose or knowing it was wrong.

- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation** — using someone else's patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret without permission (infringement is usually using it; misappropriation is usually taking or leaking a secret).

- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages** — knock-on losses that flow from the main harm (lost profits), small side costs of dealing with it, and extra money a court adds purely to punish bad behavior.

- **Cap on liability** — the maximum total dollars one side can ever be forced to pay the other under this contract, no matter how bad the damage.

- **Sole control of the defense** — the side paying the bill gets to pick the lawyers and make the calls about fighting or settling, and you step back.

- **Materially prejudiced** — your delay or mistake actually did real damage to their ability to defend, not just a technical slip-up.

Model response
## What Section 7 means in plain English

- **Both sides protect each other.** If someone outside the deal (a third party) sues or makes a claim against one party, and the claim is caused by the other party's actions (see next bullet), the party at fault must defend the other, pay the costs, and cover any resulting losses. This includes the other party's officers, employees, and agents.
- **Three triggers.** The promise applies only if the outside claim comes from: (a) the at-fault party breaking a promise or guarantee in the contract; (b) its gross negligence or intentional wrongdoing; or (c) an accusation that what it delivered (the "Deliverables") copies or misuses someone else's intellectual property.
- **The IP promise has limits.** It does not apply if the problem comes from (i) changes the other side made to the Deliverables, (ii) the other side combining them with things the provider did not supply, where the problem wouldn't have happened otherwise, or (iii) using them in a way the contract doesn't allow.
- **What you must do when sued.** Tell the other party in writing promptly. Late notice only gets them off the hook to the extent the delay actually hurt their ability to respond. You must also hand over control of the defense and settlement, and cooperate reasonably (they pay your cooperation costs).
- **Limits on their control.** They can't settle in a way that admits you did something wrong or forces you to do (or stop doing) something without your written OK. You can't unreasonably refuse.
- **No "big picture" damages, generally.** Neither side can claim indirect losses like lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, lost data, or punitive damages from the other, even if warned they could happen.
- **Dollar cap.** Each party's total liability under the whole agreement is capped at the **greater of** (A) the fees paid or owed in the 12 months before the first event that caused liability, or (B) **$100,000**.
- **Exceptions.** The bans on "big picture" damages don't apply to: indemnification obligations, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence or willful misconduct, or infringing the other party's IP. Careful: the sentence that sets the dollar cap begins "subject to the foregoing," and the wording is unclear on whether these same exceptions also lift the cap itself. Many readers would say they do not clearly do so, so have your lawyer confirm whether indemnity and confidentiality losses are capped or unlimited.

## Key terms

- **Indemnify / hold harmless:** Promise to pay for another party's losses and legal costs if a specific problem happens, and not blame them for it.
- **Third-party claim:** A demand or lawsuit from someone who is not one of the two contracting parties.
- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct:** Gross negligence is extreme carelessness, ignoring obvious risks; willful misconduct is knowingly and deliberately doing something wrong.
- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation:** Infringement is using someone's copyright, patent, or trademark without permission; misappropriation is taking or using their trade secrets or similar protected ideas improperly.
- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages:** Consequential are knock-on losses (like lost sales) that follow indirectly from a breach; incidental are minor side expenses (like the cost of finding a replacement); punitive are extra amounts meant to punish, not compensate.
- **Cap on liability:** A ceiling on the total amount one party can ever be required to pay the other.
- **Sole control of the defense:** The party paying gets to run the lawsuit, choose the lawyers, and decide strategy and settlement (within the limits above).
- **Materially prejudiced:** Seriously harmed in a way that matters, such as losing the chance to fight the claim effectively because you were told too late.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Have a lawyer review before signing.*

SECTION 7 SIMPLE TALK:

**7.1 Both sides protect each other.** If outsider sue you because I mess up, I pay. If outsider sue me because you mess up, you pay. Cover: broken promises, big-bad acts, my stuff steal someone idea. BUT me not pay if you change my stuff, mix my stuff with other stuff, or use my stuff wrong way.

- **Indemnify** = I pay your legal bill and damage cost when trouble come.

- **Defend** = I hire lawyer, fight case for you.
- **Third-party claim** = Outsider (not us two) come sue.
- **Losses** = All bad money stuff: fines, court cost, lawyer fee, damage pay.
- **Breach** = Break promise in deal.
- **Representation/warranty/covenant** = Promise you make in deal.
- **Gross negligence** = Way more sloppy than normal sloppy. Reckless.
- **Willful misconduct** = Bad thing done on purpose.
- **Infringe/misappropriate IP** = Steal or use someone patent, copyright, trademark, secret.
- **Deliverables** = Stuff one side make and hand over.
- **Tender sole control** = Hand full power over lawsuit to other side.
- **Materially prejudiced** = Real harm from late notice.
- **Indirect/consequential/incidental damages** = Ripple-effect bad stuff, not direct hit.
- **Punitive/exemplary damages** = Extra pay court add to punish.
- **Lost profits/revenue/goodwill/data** = Money not made, reputation drop, info gone.
- **Cap on liability** = Top limit on money owed.
- **Carve-outs** = Special case where cap not apply. Here: indemnify duty, secret leak, big-bad acts, IP steal.

gross negligence or willful misconduct; or (c) any allegation that the
Indemnifying Party's Deliverables, when used in accordance with this Agreement,
infringe or misappropriate any third party's intellectual property rights,
provided that the foregoing (c) shall not apply to the extent a Claim arises
from (i) modifications made by the Indemnified Parties, (ii) combination of the
Deliverables with materials not supplied by the Indemnifying Party where the
infringement would not have occurred but for such combination, or (iii) use of
the Deliverables outside the scope expressly permitted under this Agreement.

7.2 **Indemnification Procedure.** The Indemnified Parties shall (a) promptly
notify the Indemnifying Party in writing of any Claim (provided that failure to
so notify shall not relieve the Indemnifying Party of its obligations except to
the extent it is materially prejudiced thereby), (b) tender sole control of the

reasonable cooperation at the Indemnifying Party's expense.

7.3 **Limitation of Liability.** EXCEPT FOR (i) A PARTY'S INDEMNIFICATION

9, (iii) A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, OR (iv) A PARTY'S

Model response
SECTION 7 — SIMPLE TALK

BIG PICTURE
This part say: if bad thing happen and outside person sue, who pay? Also say: how much pay, max?

7.1 — PROTECT EACH OTHER (INDEMNIFICATION)
Both sides same rule. If your side mess up — break promise, act super careless or bad on purpose, or your stuff steal someone else patent/copyright — you must protect other side. Pay their lawyer, pay their loss, defend them in court.
BUT: not fair if bad thing happen because other side changed your stuff, mixed your stuff with different stuff, or used your stuff wrong way outside deal. Then you not owe protect.

Key words:
- Indemnify = you cover their loss, like shield for them.
- Indemnifying Party = side who broke thing, must shield.
- Indemnified Party = side who get hurt, gets shield.
- Claim = outside person complain/sue.
- Losses = money pain from claim — damages, fines, lawyer cost.

7.2 — HOW PROTECT WORKS (PROCEDURE)
Hurt side must tell breaker side fast, in writing, about claim. Forget tell fast? Still get shield, unless late-tell hurt breaker side bad.
Breaker side take over fight in court, make choices.
Breaker side can settle claim, but if settle say hurt-side guilty or make hurt-side do weird non-money thing — need hurt-side say okay first (and hurt-side no can say no just to be mean).
Hurt side must help when asked, breaker side pay for that help.

7.3 — MONEY CEILING (LIMITATION OF LIABILITY)
Most time: no one pay for weird indirect loss — like lost future profit, lost reputation, lost data, extra punishment money. Even if warn ahead, still no pay this kind.

Exception — these NOT capped, can pay big:
- Broke promise to shield other side (7.1 stuff)
- Leak secret info (confidentiality)
- Super careless or bad-on-purpose act
- Steal other side patent/copyright

For everything else: total pay ceiling = bigger of two number —
(A) money customer pay in last 12 month, or
(B) $100,000.
Whichever bigger, that the max. Cannot go over, except the exception list above.

SHORT VERSION FOR REGULAR PERSON
Break deal or steal idea or act reckless? You cover other guy cost, they help you fight it, you control defense. Can't dump blame-settle on them without ok. Normal mistake beyond that? Pay capped small — biggest of year fee or hundred-thousand dollar. Big-bad stuff (secret leak, steal IP, reckless act, broken shield-promise) — no cap, pay full.

UNDER ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH
DAMAGES. SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE LIABILITY
ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL NOT EXCEED THE GREATER OF

Model response
SECTION 7 — CAVEMAN SUMMARY

Big idea: each side promise cover other side when outsider sue. Then cap on how much either side owe.

7.1 — Both sides cover each other
If outsider sue you because of other side's mess, other side pay. Other side pay lawyer, pay settlement, pay fine. Covers you, your bosses, your workers.

Other side must cover when:
(a) they break promise in contract
(b) they very careless or do harm on purpose
(c) their work product get accused of stealing someone else's IP

But (c) not apply if:
- you changed their work
- you mixed their work with other stuff, and mix caused problem
- you used work in way contract not allow

7.2 — How to claim cover
When sued:
1. Tell other side fast, in writing. Tell late? Still covered, unless late hurt their case.
2. Let other side run defense and settle. But they cannot settle in way that says you guilty or makes you do things (not just pay money) without your OK. You not say no without good reason.
3. Help them. They pay cost of help.

7.3 — Cap on blame money
Two rules:

Rule one: no side pay other for indirect harm. No lost profit. No lost revenue. No lost reputation. No lost data. Even if warned harm might happen.

Rule two: total money one side owe other, whole contract, capped at bigger of:
(A) fees customer paid or owe provider in 12 months before first bad event, or
(B) $100,000.

Caps not apply for four things:
- 7.1 cover duty
- breaking secrecy (Section 9)
- very careless or on-purpose harm
- stealing other side's IP

So those four? No cap. Full blame money.

KEY WORDS, PLAIN

Indemnify: "I pay if you get sued for my mess." Insurance-like promise.

Hold harmless: "I will not let this hurt you." Goes with indemnify.

Defend: pay for and run lawyers in court fight.

Indemnifying Party: side doing paying.

Indemnified Parties: side getting protected, plus their bosses, workers, agents.

Third-party claim: outsider sue. Not you vs. me. Someone else vs. one of us.

Claims: lawsuits, demands, legal actions from outsider.

Losses: all cost that come from Claim. Money paid, fines, lawyer bills.

Representation / warranty / covenant: promise in contract. Rep = "this is true." Warranty = "I guarantee this." Covenant = "I will do this."

Gross negligence: very very careless. Way past normal mistake.

Willful misconduct: did bad thing on purpose.

Deliverables: work product one side hand over.

Intellectual property (IP): ideas someone own. Patents, copyright, trademarks, secrets.

Infringe / misappropriate: infringe = use someone's IP without OK. Misappropriate = take secret wrongly.

Materially prejudiced: actually hurt in real way. Not small hurt.

Tender sole control: hand over full control. Other side drives.

Consent not unreasonably withheld: you can say no, but only with real reason.

Indirect / consequential damages: harm that flow from harm. Not direct hit. Example: broken software (direct) make you lose customer (consequential).

Incidental damages: side costs from problem.

Special damages: unusual losses tied to your situation.

Punitive / exemplary damages: extra money court add to punish, not to repay.

Theory of liability: legal path used to blame. Contract, negligence, etc. Cap block all paths.

Cumulative liability: all blame money added up, whole contract life.

Greater of A or B: pick bigger number. Floor is $100,000. Can be more if 12-month fees bigger.

WHY CARE
- Sued by outsider for other side's fault? They pay.
- Sued for your own fault? You pay, not them.
- Most money you owe: 12 months fees or $100K, bigger one. Except four no-cap cases.
- No lost-profit money, ever, except four no-cap cases.
- Get sued? Tell other side fast. Let them run defense. Help them.

Model response
**Big point:** Both sides must cover other side for some outside claims they cause. But most other money risk gets capped, and many kinds of extra damages get blocked.

**Plain talk summary**
1. **Both sides owe backup** if own bad act causes outside claim. If one side breaks promises in contract, acts with very bad carelessness, does harm on purpose, or gives work/product that wrongly uses someone else’s IP, that side must step in, handle claim, and pay related costs.
2. **IP claim has limits.** No cover if other side changed deliverable, mixed it with other stuff not given by provider, or used it in way contract did not allow.
3. **Claim process:** Hurt side must give fast written notice, let other side control defense and settlement, and help as needed. But settling has limit: defending side cannot make other side admit fault or take non-money duties unless other side says yes in writing.
4. **Liability cap:** Most contract claims cannot go past higher of:
   - fees paid/payable in prior 12 months, or
   - **$100,000**
5. **Some losses not recoverable:** No indirect or extra damages like lost profits, lost revenue, lost goodwill, or lost data.
6. **Big exceptions:** Damage limits do **not** protect side from:
   - indemnity duties in 7.1
   - confidentiality breaches
   - gross negligence
   - willful misconduct
   - infringing other side’s IP

**Key legal words, plain**
| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Pay back or protect other side from loss or claim |
| **Defend** | Take over legal defense, like hiring lawyers and fighting claim |
| **Hold harmless** | Keep other side from having pay for harm covered here |
| **Indemnifying Party** | Side who must protect/pay |
| **Indemnified Parties** | Side getting protection, plus its people like staff, officers, agents |
| **Third-party claim** | Claim from outsider, not one of two contract sides |
| **Claim** | Demand, lawsuit, or legal case |
| **Losses** | Money harm: damages, settlements, judgments, fines, legal fees, other costs |
| **Representation / warranty / covenant** | Contract promise: fact stated true, promise about quality, or promise do/not do something |
| **Gross negligence** | Very serious carelessness, far worse than normal mistake |
| **Willful misconduct** | Wrong act done on purpose, or with knowing disregard |
| **Deliverables** | Work, product, files, software, or other items one side must provide |
| **Infringe / misappropriate IP** | Use someone else’s patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, or other IP without right |
| **Materially prejudiced** | Truly harmed in meaningful way by delay or failure, not just annoyed |
| **Sole control of defense** | One side alone runs legal strategy and lawyer work |
| **Settle** | End claim by agreement, often with payment or other terms |
| **Non-monetary obligation** | Duty not about money, like admit fault, stop doing something, or change behavior |
| **Limitation of liability** | Rule capping how much money one side can owe |
| **Indirect / consequential / special / punitive damages** | Extra or knock-on losses, not direct bill; can include business fallout or punishment-style damages |
| **Cumulative liability** | Total max amount owed from all covered claims together |

**Bottom line:** Contract says, “You break it or cause outside claim, you handle it.” But for most other disputes, money exposure stays limited and many big business-loss claims get cut off.

# Section 7 — Caveman Version

## 7.1 Both Side Cover Each Other
If outsider attack you because *my* mistake, I pay. Mistakes count:
- I break promise I made in deal
- I act very reckless or do bad thing on purpose
- My work steps on someone else's idea-rights

But NOT my problem if:
- You change my work yourself
- You bolt my work onto other stuff I no give you, and *that* cause problem
- You use my work in way deal no allow

Same rule both way. You mess up, you pay.

## 7.2 How Cover Work
You get attacked, you must:
1. Tell me fast, in writing. (Slow telling no kill my duty — unless slow really hurt my defense.)
2. Hand me wheel. I run fight, I run settle. But I no sign deal that say YOU guilty, or force YOU do something, unless you say ok. You no refuse ok for dumb reason.
3. Help me when I ask. I pay for your help time.

## 7.3 Damage Cap
**Big rule:** Neither side pay for ripple-damage — lost money, lost future deals, lost good name, lost data. Even if warned it might happen.

**Money ceiling:** Total pay never more than bigger of:
- fees Customer paid Provider in 12 months before trouble start, OR
- $100,000

**Cap NOT apply** (no ceiling, full pain) when:
- cover-duty from 7.1
- secret-spilling under Section 9
- very reckless or on-purpose bad act
- one side steal other side idea-rights

---

# Word Meanings

| Big word | Caveman meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | I pay your bill when my mess hurt you |
| **Defend** | I hire lawyer, I fight case for you |
| **Hold harmless** | You walk away clean, no cost |
| **Third-party claim** | Outsider — not you, not me — come swinging |
| **Representation / warranty** | Promise fact true |
| **Covenant** | Promise do thing (or not do thing) |
| **Gross negligence** | Way past sloppy. Reckless |
| **Willful misconduct** | Knew bad, did anyway |
| **Infringe** | Step on someone patent/copyright/trademark |
| **Misappropriate** | Take secret not yours |
| **Materially prejudiced** | Real harm, not paper-cut harm |
| **Tender control of defense** | Give me driver seat in lawsuit |
| **Indirect / consequential damages** | Ripple harm, not first hit |
| **Punitive / exemplary damages** | Extra pain money, punish-money |
| **Loss of goodwill** | Name get muddy, people trust less |
| **Total cumulative liability** | All pay added up, whole deal life |
| **Carve-out** (the "EXCEPT FOR") | Hole in shield. Cap no protect here |

---

**Two things watch close:**
1. Carve-outs in 7.3 big. Cover-duty and secret-spilling have NO ceiling. Real money risk live there, not in $100k cap.
2. Cap say "greater of" — good for Customer. Small deal still get $100k floor.

2. Give other side full control of fight and deal. But other side can't settle by admitting fault, or forcing non-money duty, without written OK (OK can't be unreasonably refused).
3. Help, at paying side's cost.

**7.3 Cap on how much you pay.**
- **No** payment for side-effect losses: lost profit, lost sales, lost reputation, lost data, punishment damages. Even if warned.
- **Exceptions** (no protection, no cap): indemnity duties, secrecy breach (Section 9), gross negligence or willful wrongdoing, IP theft.
- Other losses capped. Max total per side = **bigger of**: fees paid/owed in last 12 months, or **$100,000**.

*Note: Text says exceptions escape only the side-effect ban ("Subject to the foregoing"). Cap wording unclear whether exceptions also escape cap. Ask lawyer.*

## Key Terms

- **Indemnify:** Pay other side back for loss from outside claim.
- **Hold harmless:** Not blame other side, not make them pay.
- **Indemnifying Party:** Side who pays.
- **Indemnified Parties:** Side protected, plus staff.
- **Claim:** Outside person's demand or lawsuit.
- **Losses:** Money owed: damages, fines, legal fees.
- **Third party:** Someone not in contract.
- **Breach:** Break contract promise.
- **Representation/warranty/covenant:** Statement of fact / guarantee / promise to do or not do.
- **Gross negligence:** Very reckless, far worse than normal mistake.
- **Willful misconduct:** Bad act done on purpose.
- **Deliverables:** Things one side must hand over.
- **Infringe/misappropriate:** Copy or take IP without right.
- **Intellectual property (IP):** Ideas, code, brands, patents, copyrights.
- **Materially prejudiced:** Really hurt by delay.
- **Tender control:** Hand over command of defense.
- **Indirect/consequential damages:** Loss that come later as side-effect, not direct.
- **Punitive/exemplary damages:** Extra money to punish.
- **Goodwill:** Good name, customer trust.
- **Cumulative liability:** Total of all payments, added up.

7.1 **Mutual Indemnification.** Each Party (the "Indemnifying Party") shall
defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the other Party and its officers,
directors, employees, and agents (the "Indemnified Parties") from and against
any and all third-party claims, demands, actions, suits, or proceedings

    <h1>Section 7 &mdash; Indemnification &amp; Limitation of Liability</h1>
    <p class="subtitle">Who covers whom when something goes wrong, and how much money is on the line.</p>

  <div class="task">
    <strong>The task:</strong> Summarize Section 7 of the contract for a non-lawyer, and translate the key legal terms into plain English.

  <h2>The Short Version</h2>
  <p>
    Section 7 does two related things. First, it says that if a third party sues one of the parties because of something the <em>other</em> party did (like breaking a promise in the contract, being seriously careless, or shipping something that infringes someone's patent or copyright), the party at fault has to step in, take over the lawsuit, and pay the bill.
  </p>
  <p>
    Second, it puts a hard ceiling on the kinds of damages and the total dollar amount either party can be forced to pay under this contract &mdash; with a few important exceptions that break through that ceiling.
  </p>

  <h2>7.1 &mdash; Who Pays When Someone Else Sues</h2>
  <p>Each party promises to protect the other from third-party lawsuits that arise from three specific things:</p>
  <ol>
    <li><strong>Broken promises</strong> &mdash; a party breaks a representation, warranty, or covenant in the contract.</li>
    <li><strong>Serious misconduct</strong> &mdash; a party is grossly negligent or intentionally does something wrong.</li>
    <li><strong>IP infringement</strong> &mdash; a party's Deliverables (the work product it hands over) allegedly infringe someone else's intellectual property.</li>
  </ol>
  <p>The IP promise has three carve-outs. The infringing party does <em>not</em> owe protection if the problem was caused by:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>The other side modifying the Deliverables,</li>
    <li>The other side combining the Deliverables with something else that caused the infringement, or</li>
    <li>The other side using the Deliverables in a way the contract didn't allow.</li>
  </ul>

  <h2>7.2 &mdash; How the Process Works</h2>
  <p>If a covered lawsuit shows up, the party being sued must:</p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Give prompt written notice</strong> to the party that owes protection (though a late notice only hurts them if the delay actually caused real harm to the defense).</li>
    <li><strong>Hand over the driver's seat</strong> &mdash; let the indemnifying party run the defense and negotiate any settlement. But that party can't agree to a settlement that admits fault or forces the other side to <em>do</em> something (as opposed to just paying money) without written permission.</li>
    <li><strong>Cooperate reasonably</strong>, with expenses covered by the party running the defense.</li>
  </ul>

  <h2>7.3 &mdash; The Cap on Damages</h2>
  <p>This is written in all-caps in the original for a reason: it's the money-limiting clause. It has two parts.</p>

  <h3>Part A: No indirect damages</h3>
  <p>Neither party can sue the other for &ldquo;soft&rdquo; damages &mdash; things like lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, or lost data &mdash; even if the other side was warned that those losses might happen.</p>

  <h3>Part B: A total dollar ceiling</h3>
  <p>The most either party can owe the other, in total, is the larger of:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>The fees the Customer paid (or owes) in the <strong>12 months before</strong> the problem started, or</li>
    <li><strong>$100,000</strong>.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="callout">
    <strong>Important: the cap has holes.</strong>
    Both the &ldquo;no indirect damages&rdquo; rule and the dollar cap do <em>not</em> apply to: (i) the indemnification obligations in 7.1, (ii) breaches of confidentiality (Section 9), (iii) gross negligence or willful misconduct, or (iv) infringing the other party's intellectual property. For any of those, a party can be on the hook for the full amount of the harm.
  </div>

      <tr><th>Situation</th><th>Is there a $ cap?</th><th>Are indirect damages allowed?</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Ordinary contract dispute</td><td>Yes &mdash; greater of 12 months' fees or $100K</td><td>No</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Indemnified third-party claim (7.1)</td><td>No cap</td><td>Yes (as awarded)</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Confidentiality breach</td><td>No cap</td><td>Yes</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Gross negligence or willful misconduct</td><td>No cap</td><td>Yes</td></tr>
      <tr><td>IP infringement of the other party's rights</td><td>No cap</td><td>Yes</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>

  <h2>Key Legal Terms in Plain Language</h2>
  <dl class="glossary">
    <dt>Indemnify</dt>
    <dd>To promise, in advance, that you'll cover another party's losses if a specific kind of trouble happens &mdash; and usually to handle the fight yourself.</dd>

    <dt>Defend, indemnify, and hold harmless</dt>
    <dd>The full package: (1) show up and run the legal defense, (2) pay any damages or settlement, and (3) make sure the protected party ends up no worse off financially.</dd>

    <dt>Indemnifying Party / Indemnified Party</dt>
    <dd>The one making the promise to protect (Indemnifying) versus the one being protected (Indemnified).</dd>

    <dt>Third-party claim</dt>
    <dd>A lawsuit or demand brought by someone <em>outside</em> the contract &mdash; not by the other party themselves.</dd>

    <dt>Representation, warranty, or covenant</dt>
    <dd>Three kinds of contractual promises. A <em>representation</em> is a statement of fact; a <em>warranty</em> is a guarantee that something is or will be true; a <em>covenant</em> is a promise to do (or not do) something.</dd>

    <dt>Gross negligence</dt>
    <dd>Carelessness that goes well beyond an ordinary mistake &mdash; a reckless disregard for obvious risks.</dd>

    <dt>Willful misconduct</dt>
    <dd>Deliberately doing something wrong, or acting with knowledge that harm will likely result.</dd>

    <dt>Infringe / misappropriate</dt>
    <dd><em>Infringe</em> means using someone's protected work (patent, copyright, trademark) without permission. <em>Misappropriate</em> usually refers to improperly taking or using a trade secret.</dd>

    <dt>Deliverables</dt>
    <dd>The tangible things one party hands over under the contract &mdash; software, documents, reports, designs, etc.</dd>

    <dt>Tender sole control of the defense</dt>
    <dd>Formally hand over the lawsuit &mdash; the party that owes indemnification picks the lawyers and calls the shots.</dd>

    <dt>Materially prejudiced</dt>
    <dd>Actually and significantly harmed &mdash; not just inconvenienced. Late notice only excuses the indemnifier if the delay caused real damage to the defense.</dd>

    <dt>Not to be unreasonably withheld</dt>
    <dd>A party has to say yes unless they have a genuinely good reason to say no; they can't refuse just to be difficult.</dd>

    <dt>Indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages</dt>
    <dd>Categories of damages that go beyond the immediate, direct loss. Examples: lost future profits, harm to reputation, or punishment-style awards. The clause blocks all of these.</dd>

    <dt>Under any theory of liability</dt>
    <dd>No matter what legal argument someone tries &mdash; contract, negligence, statute, etc. &mdash; the same limit applies.</dd>

    <dt>Even if advised of the possibility of such damages</dt>
    <dd>The cap holds even if the other party warned in advance that these losses could happen. Warning doesn't create liability.</dd>

    <dt>Total cumulative liability</dt>
    <dd>Everything added up together &mdash; not per claim, not per year. Once the cap is hit, it's hit for the life of the contract.</dd>

    <dt>Fees paid or payable</dt>
    <dd>Money already paid <em>plus</em> money owed but not yet paid. Both count toward the 12-month total used to calculate the cap.</dd>
  </dl>

  <footer>
    This is a plain-language summary intended to aid understanding. It is not legal advice and does not replace the contract's actual language, which controls in any dispute.
