    If Party A causes a problem, Party A has to step in, handle the legal defense, and cover the resulting costs for Party B — and vice versa.
    This protection kicks in when the problem comes from one of three sources:
  </p>
  <ul>
    <li>The party broke a promise it made in the contract.</li>
    <li>The party did something seriously careless or intentionally wrong.</li>
    <li>The party's deliverable (software, product, work product, etc.) is accused of stealing or infringing someone else's intellectual property — <em>but only if the deliverable was used the way the contract intended.</em> If the other side modified it, mixed it with outside materials, or used it beyond what was agreed, that protection doesn't apply.</li>
  </ul>

  <h3>7.2 — The Ground Rules for Handling a Claim</h3>
  <p>
    If you're the one being protected and a claim comes in, you must tell the other party promptly (though a late notice only hurts you if it actually caused them harm).
    You then hand over control of the legal defense to them — they run the case, not you.
    The one guardrail: they can't settle in a way that admits you did something wrong or forces you to do something (as opposed to just paying money) without your sign-off.
    You're expected to cooperate along the way, and they cover what that cooperation costs.
  </p>

  <h3>7.3 — The Payout Ceiling</h3>
  <p>
    This is the section written in all capital letters, which is standard practice for making sure a limitation of liability clause is legally enforceable and hard to miss.
    It does two things:
  </p>
  <ol>
    <li><strong>Blocks certain damage types entirely.</strong> Neither side can collect "indirect" losses — things like lost profits, lost business reputation, or lost data — even if those losses were foreseeable and even if the other side knew they might happen.</li>
    <li><strong>Caps total liability.</strong> Beyond that, each party's total responsibility for anything related to the contract is capped at whichever is larger: the fees paid in the last 12 months, or $100,000.</li>
  </ol>
  <div class="callout">
    <strong>The big exception:</strong> none of these limits apply to the indemnification promises from 7.1, breaches of confidentiality, gross negligence or willful misconduct, or IP infringement. Those four categories carry uncapped exposure — they carve straight through the liability shield.
  </div>

  <h2>Key Legal Terms Defined</h2>
  <dl class="term-list">
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Indemnify / Indemnification</dt>
      <dd>To compensate someone for a loss, and to take responsibility for defending them if they get sued over it. Think of it as an insurance-like promise between the two contracting parties themselves.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Hold Harmless</dt>
      <dd>A promise not to let the other party suffer financial harm — usually paired with "indemnify" as a single combined obligation.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Third-Party Claim</dt>
      <dd>A lawsuit or legal demand brought by someone <em>outside</em> the contract — not a dispute between the two companies that signed the agreement, but a customer, competitor, or other outsider suing one of them.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Gross Negligence</dt>
      <dd>Carelessness far beyond an honest mistake — a serious, reckless disregard for consequences that a reasonable person would clearly recognize as dangerous or wrong.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Willful Misconduct</dt>
      <dd>Doing something harmful on purpose, or with knowledge that harm was highly likely — as opposed to an accident or an oversight.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Misappropriate (Intellectual Property)</dt>
      <dd>To use someone else's protected creation — a patent, trademark, trade secret, or copyrighted work — without permission.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Tender Control of Defense</dt>
      <dd>To hand over the steering wheel of a lawsuit to the other party — they choose the lawyers, the strategy, and generally the outcome.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Consequential / Indirect Damages</dt>
      <dd>Losses that are a knock-on effect of a problem, rather than the direct cost of fixing it — e.g., losing a big customer contract because a product broke, rather than just the cost of the broken product itself.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Punitive / Exemplary Damages</dt>
      <dd>Money a court awards not to compensate a loss, but to punish especially bad behavior and discourage others from doing the same thing.</dd>
    </div>
    <div class="term">
      <dt>Limitation of Liability</dt>
      <dd>A contract clause that caps how much one party can ever be forced to pay the other, no matter how large the actual damages turn out to be.</dd>
    </div>
  </dl>

  <h2>Quick Reference: What's Capped vs. Uncapped</h2>
  <table>
    <tr><th>Type of Loss</th><th>Subject to the $100k / 12-month Cap?</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Indirect, incidental, consequential, punitive damages; lost profits, revenue, goodwill, or data</td><td>Excluded entirely — never recoverable, capped or not</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Ordinary breach-of-contract damages (general/direct losses)</td><td>Yes — subject to the cap</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Indemnification obligations (Section 7.1)</td><td>No cap</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Confidentiality breaches (Section 9)</td><td>No cap</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Gross negligence or willful misconduct</td><td>No cap</td></tr>
    <tr><td>IP infringement by a party</td><td>No cap</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="disclaimer">
    This summary is provided for general understanding only and is not legal advice. Contract language like this can have significant financial consequences, and small wording differences can change outcomes substantially — consult a qualified attorney before relying on this interpretation.
  </div>

  <p style="color:var(--muted)">Indemnification and Limitation of Liability</p>

  <div class="task">

    <pre>7.1 Mutual Indemnification. 7.3 Limitation of Liability. EXCEPT FOR (i) A PARTY'S INDEMNIFICATION OBLIGATIONS UNDER SECTION 7.1, (ii) BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY UNDER SECTION 9, (iii) A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, OR (iv) A PARTY'S INFRINGEMENT OF THE OTHER PARTY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, SPECIAL, PUNITIVE, OR EXEMPLARY DAMAGES, OR FOR ANY LOST PROFITS, LOST REVENUE, LOSS OF GOODWILL, OR LOSS OF DATA, HOWEVER CAUSED AND UNDER ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGES. SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE LIABILITY ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL NOT EXCEED THE GREATER OF (A) THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER TO PROVIDER UNDER THIS AGREEMENT IN THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS PRECEDING THE FIRST EVENT GIVING RISE TO LIABILITY, OR (B) ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND U.S. DOLLARS ($100,000).</pre>
  </details>

  <h2>The one-paragraph version</h2>
  <p>
    Section 7 answers two questions: <em>who pays when an outsider sues one of us because of something the other one did</em>, and <em>how much can we owe each other if things go wrong between us</em>. The answer to the first is: the side that caused the problem covers the other side's costs, with a set procedure for handling the lawsuit. The answer to the second is: neither side pays the other for indirect or speculative harms like lost profits, and each side's total exposure is capped at the last twelve months of fees or $100,000, whichever is larger. A few serious kinds of misconduct are carved out of the cap and can lead to unlimited liability.
  </p>

  <h2>Section by section</h2>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="label">7.1</span>
    <h3>Mutual Indemnification: "If your actions get me sued, you cover it."</h3>
    <p>
      This works in both directions. If a third party (someone who is not a party to this contract) brings a claim against one side, and that claim is caused by the <em>other</em> side, the side at fault must defend the lawsuit and pay the resulting costs. That includes damages, settlements, fines, and reasonable outside lawyer fees. The protection extends to the company's officers, directors, employees, and agents, not just the company itself.
    </p>
    <p>The obligation is triggered in three situations:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Breaking a promise in the contract.</strong> A party broke a representation, warranty, or covenant it made in the agreement.</li>
      <li><strong>Serious carelessness or intentional wrongdoing.</strong> Not ordinary mistakes; this is gross negligence or willful misconduct.</li>
      <li><strong>Intellectual property infringement.</strong> Someone claims that the party's Deliverables (the work product it supplied) violate their patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret.</li>
    </ul>
    <p>The IP protection has three exceptions. The supplying party does <em>not</em> have to cover an IP claim to the extent the problem was created by the other side:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>the other side modified the Deliverables;</li>
      <li>the other side combined the Deliverables with something else, and the combination is what caused the infringement; or</li>
      <li>the other side used the Deliverables in a way the contract does not allow.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="label">7.2</span>
    <h3>Indemnification Procedure: "Here's how we handle the lawsuit."</h3>
    <p>When a covered claim comes in, the side being protected has three duties:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Tell the other side promptly, in writing.</strong> Being late does not forfeit the protection unless the delay actually hurt the other side's ability to defend the case.</li>
      <li><strong>Hand over control of the defense.</strong> The paying side gets to run the lawsuit and decide whether to settle. One limit: it cannot agree to a settlement that says the protected side did something wrong, or that forces the protected side to do anything other than have money paid on its behalf, without the protected side's written permission. That permission cannot be withheld for unreasonable reasons.</li>
      <li><strong>Cooperate reasonably.</strong> Provide documents, witnesses, and so on. The paying side reimburses the costs of that cooperation.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="label">7.3</span>
    <h3>Limitation of Liability: "Here's the most either of us can owe the other."</h3>
    <p>This clause is written in all capitals because courts in many places require limitation clauses to be conspicuous. It does two things.</p>
    <p><strong>First, it excludes certain types of damages entirely.</strong> Neither side can recover from the other for indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages, or for lost profits, lost revenue, loss of goodwill, or loss of data. This holds no matter how the harm happened or what legal theory is used, even if the other side was warned it could happen.</p>
    <p><strong>Second, it caps total liability.</strong> Everything a party could owe the other under this agreement, added together, cannot exceed the <em>greater</em> of:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>the fees the Customer paid or owes the Provider in the twelve months before the first event that caused the liability, or</li>
      <li>$100,000.</li>
    </ul>
    <p>The cap and the exclusions <strong>do not apply</strong> to four things, which means liability for these can be unlimited:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>the indemnification obligations in 7.1;</li>
      <li>breaches of the confidentiality section (Section 9);</li>
      <li>gross negligence or willful misconduct; and</li>
      <li>one party infringing the other party's intellectual property.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div class="callout">
    <strong>Something worth noticing.</strong> The cap is measured by fees the Customer pays the Provider. In a typical year that number is the same for both sides, so the cap is symmetric in dollars. But the carve-outs matter more than the cap in practice: an IP indemnity claim or a confidentiality breach can cost far more than twelve months of fees, and those are exactly the items left uncapped.
  </div>

  <h2>Quick reference</h2>
  <div class="table-wrap">
  <table>
    <thead>
      <tr><th>Question</th><th>Answer under Section 7</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Who covers a third-party lawsuit?</td><td>The party whose breach, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or infringing Deliverables caused it.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Who runs the defense?</td><td>The paying party, but it needs consent to settle in a way that admits fault or imposes non-money obligations on the other side.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Can I recover lost profits from the other side?</td><td>No, unless the claim falls under one of the four carve-outs.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>What is the maximum I can owe?</td><td>The greater of the last 12 months of fees or $100,000, except for the four carve-outs, which are uncapped.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>What is uncapped?</td><td>Indemnification duties, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence or willful misconduct, and infringing the other side's IP.</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>

  <h2>Key terms, defined plainly</h2>
  <dl>
    <dt>Indemnify</dt>
    <dd>To reimburse someone for a loss. If you indemnify me, you pay the costs I incur because of a covered problem.</dd>

    <dt>Hold harmless</dt>
    <dd>A promise not to hold someone responsible for a loss, and to shield them from it. Usually paired with "indemnify"; together they mean "you will not end up out of pocket for this."</dd>

    <dt>Defend</dt>
    <dd>To take on the actual lawsuit: hire the lawyers, manage the case, and pay for it. This is a separate duty from paying the eventual judgment.</dd>

    <dt>Indemnifying Party / Indemnified Parties</dt>
    <dd>The Indemnifying Party is the side that pays. The Indemnified Parties are the side being protected, along with its officers, directors, employees, and agents.</dd>

    <dt>Third-party claim</dt>
    <dd>A lawsuit or demand from someone who is not a party to this contract. Section 7.1 only applies to these, not to disputes between the two contracting parties themselves.</dd>

    <dt>Claims / Losses</dt>
    <dd>"Claims" is the contract's shorthand for lawsuits, demands, and legal proceedings. "Losses" is shorthand for everything those Claims end up costing: damages, settlements, judgments, fines, penalties, and reasonable outside lawyer fees.</dd>

    <dt>Representation, warranty, covenant</dt>
    <dd>Three kinds of promises in a contract. A representation is a statement of fact ("we own this software"). A warranty is a guarantee that something is or will be true ("the software will work as described"). A covenant is a promise to do or not do something ("we will keep your data confidential").</dd>

    <dt>Gross negligence</dt>
    <dd>Carelessness so severe it shows a reckless disregard for the consequences. Ordinary mistakes are simple negligence; gross negligence is a much higher bar.</dd>

    <dt>Willful misconduct</dt>
    <dd>Doing something wrong on purpose, or knowing it is wrong and doing it anyway.</dd>

    <dt>Deliverables</dt>
    <dd>The work product one party supplies to the other under the contract: software, documents, designs, and so on. Defined elsewhere in the agreement.</dd>

    <dt>Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property</dt>
    <dd>To use someone else's patent, copyright, or trademark without permission (infringe), or to take and use their trade secrets improperly (misappropriate).</dd>

    <dt>Materially prejudiced</dt>
    <dd>Actually harmed in a meaningful way. Here it means the delay in notifying the paying party genuinely hurt its ability to defend the case, for example because evidence was lost or a deadline was missed.</dd>

    <dt>Tender control of the defense</dt>
    <dd>To hand over the running of the lawsuit to the other party, so they choose the lawyers, set the strategy, and decide on settlement.</dd>

    <dt>Consent not to be unreasonably withheld</dt>
    <dd>You can say no, but only for a legitimate reason. You cannot refuse just to be difficult or to gain leverage.</dd>

    <dt>Direct vs. indirect (consequential) damages</dt>
    <dd>Direct damages are the immediate, predictable cost of a breach, such as the cost of fixing or replacing what was promised. Indirect or consequential damages are the downstream effects, such as the business you lost because the thing was late. Section 7.3 lets you recover the first kind but not the second.</dd>

    <dt>Incidental damages</dt>
    <dd>Smaller costs incurred while dealing with a breach, such as the expense of inspecting defective goods or arranging a substitute.</dd>

    <dt>Special damages</dt>
    <dd>Losses that arise from a party's particular circumstances rather than from the breach in general. Often treated as a subset of consequential damages.</dd>

    <dt>Punitive / exemplary damages</dt>
    <dd>Money a court awards to punish bad behavior and deter others, on top of compensating the actual loss. Both words mean the same thing.</dd>

    <dt>Loss of goodwill</dt>
    <dd>Damage to a company's reputation or customer relationships, as distinct from a direct out-of-pocket cost.</dd>

    <dt>Theory of liability</dt>
    <dd>The legal basis for a claim: breach of contract, negligence, strict liability, and so on. "Under any theory of liability" means the exclusion applies no matter which legal route the claim takes.</dd>

    <dt>Total cumulative liability</dt>
    <dd>Everything a party owes the other under the contract, added up across all claims over the life of the agreement. The cap is not per incident; it is one ceiling for everything combined.</dd>

    <dt>Carve-out</dt>
    <dd>An exception written into a limitation. The four items listed at the start of 7.3 are carve-outs: the cap and the exclusions do not apply to them.</dd>
  </dl>

  <footer>
    This is a plain-language explanation for orientation, not legal advice. How these provisions apply to a specific situation depends on the rest of the agreement and the governing law, and should be reviewed with a lawyer.
  </footer>
</main>
</body>
</html>

    <h1>Plain-English Summary of Section 7 — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability</h1>

    <div class="note">
      <p><strong>Overall meaning:</strong> This section says when one side has to protect the other from outside legal claims, how that process works, and how much each side can be financially responsible for if something goes wrong.</p>
    </div>

    <h2>Simple Summary</h2>
    <p>Both parties agree to protect the other if a third party makes certain kinds of legal claims. If one party breaks the agreement, acts with serious carelessness, acts intentionally wrong, or provides work that wrongly uses someone else’s intellectual property, that party must cover the other side’s related losses and legal costs.</p>

    <p>There are limits to that protection. A party does not have to cover an intellectual property claim if the other side changed the deliverables, combined them with outside materials that caused the problem, or used them in a way the agreement did not allow.</p>

    <p>If a claim happens, the protected party must notify the other side promptly, let that other side control the defense and settlement, and reasonably help with the case. But the defending party cannot settle in a way that admits fault for the protected party or forces the protected party to do something non-monetary unless the protected party agrees in writing.</p>

    <p>The contract also limits liability. In most cases, neither side can recover indirect or hard-to-measure damages like lost profits, lost revenue, lost goodwill, or lost data. Also, except for certain serious categories, each party’s total financial liability is capped at the higher of:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>the fees the customer paid or owed in the 12 months before the first event that caused liability, or</li>
      <li>$100,000.</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The liability cap and damage exclusions do <strong>not</strong> apply to certain important issues, including indemnification duties, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence, willful misconduct, and infringement of the other party’s intellectual property rights.</p>

    <h2>What This Means in Practical Terms</h2>
    <ul>
      <li>If one side causes a serious legal problem, that side generally pays for the fallout.</li>
      <li>The protected side must hand over control of the legal defense, with some safeguards.</li>
      <li>Big categories of knock-on damages are excluded in most disputes.</li>
      <li>Most financial exposure is capped, but the cap does not protect a party from the most serious types of wrongdoing listed in the section.</li>
    </ul>

    <h2>Key Legal Terms in Plain Language</h2>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Indemnify:</span> To pay the other side back, or protect them financially, for certain claims, losses, or damages.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Defend:</span> To take responsibility for handling the legal defense of a claim, usually including hiring lawyers and managing the case.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Hold harmless:</span> To shield the other side from having to bear the cost or legal burden of a covered claim.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Indemnifying Party:</span> The party that must defend and pay when a covered claim falls within its responsibility.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Indemnified Parties:</span> The people or entities being protected, including the other party and its officers, directors, employees, and agents.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Third-party claim:</span> A claim brought by someone outside the contract, not by one of the two parties to the agreement.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Representation:</span> A statement of fact one party says is true.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Warranty:</span> A promise that certain facts, conditions, or performance standards are true or will be met.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Covenant:</span> A promise in the contract that a party will do, or not do, something.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Gross negligence:</span> More than ordinary carelessness; a very serious failure to use reasonable care.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Willful misconduct:</span> Intentional wrongdoing, or acting with knowing disregard for the likely harm.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Deliverables:</span> The work product, materials, software, documents, or other items one party provides under the agreement.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property:</span> To improperly use, copy, or take someone else’s protected creations, such as copyrights, patents, trademarks, or trade secrets.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Scope expressly permitted under this Agreement:</span> The specific ways the contract says the deliverables may be used. Using them outside those allowed ways can remove protection.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Promptly notify:</span> Inform the other side without unreasonable delay.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Materially prejudiced:</span> Meaningfully harmed in a practical way. Here, late notice only excuses the defending party if the delay actually hurt its ability to handle the claim.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Sole control of the defense and settlement:</span> One party gets to manage the lawsuit and settlement discussions by itself, subject to the limits stated in the contract.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Non-monetary obligation:</span> A requirement to do something other than pay money, such as admit fault, change business practices, or stop using something.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages:</span> Categories of damages that go beyond direct out-of-pocket harm, such as ripple-effect losses, penalties, or punishment-style awards.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Lost profits / lost revenue / loss of goodwill / loss of data:</span> Financial or business harm from missed earnings, damaged reputation, or missing information.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Total cumulative liability:</span> The maximum total amount one party can owe under the agreement for covered claims, added together.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="term">
      <p><span class="label">Liability cap:</span> The contractual maximum amount one party can be required to pay, except where the contract says the cap does not apply.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

<h2>The Short Version</h2>
<div class="bottom-line">
  <strong>In one paragraph:</strong>
  If someone outside this contract sues you because of something the other side did wrong, the other side has to step in, run the lawsuit, and pay the bill — and the same rule applies in reverse. In exchange, both sides agree to cap how much they can ever owe each other: no payment for knock-on business losses like lost profits, and a hard ceiling of either the last 12 months of fees or $100,000, whichever is larger. That cap does <em>not</em> apply to the worst categories of misconduct.
</div>

<h2>Clause by Clause</h2>

<h3><span class="clause">7.1</span> Who covers whom</h3>
<p>Each side promises to protect the other from lawsuits brought by outsiders. "Protect" here means three things bundled together: hire the lawyers and run the defense, pay whatever comes out of it (judgments, settlements, fines, legal fees), and make sure the other side doesn't end up out of pocket.</p>
<p>This protection kicks in for three kinds of problems:</p>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Broken promises.</strong> You said something in the contract and it turned out to be untrue, or you agreed to do something and didn't.</li>
  <li><strong>Serious misbehavior.</strong> Not ordinary mistakes — this covers reckless carelessness or doing something wrong on purpose.</li>
  <li><strong>Stolen or copied intellectual property.</strong> Someone claims the work you delivered uses their patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret without permission.</li>
</ul>
<p>The IP protection has three escape hatches. The provider is off the hook if the customer <strong>changed</strong> the delivered work, <strong>bolted it onto something else</strong> the provider never supplied and that combination is what caused the problem, or <strong>used it in a way the contract doesn't allow</strong>. In short: you're covered when you use the thing as intended, not when you modify it or go off-script.</p>

<h3><span class="clause">7.2</span> The rules for asking for help</h3>
<p>Protection isn't automatic — the side being sued has to follow three steps:</p>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Tell them quickly, in writing.</strong> A late notice doesn't cancel the protection unless the delay genuinely damaged the other side's ability to defend the case.</li>
  <li><strong>Hand over the steering wheel.</strong> The side paying for the defense gets to run it and decide whether to settle. The trade-off: they can't agree to a settlement that admits <em>you</em> did something wrong, or that forces <em>you</em> to do something beyond writing a check, without your written OK — and you can't refuse that OK for no good reason.</li>
  <li><strong>Help out.</strong> Turn over documents, make people available, and so on. The other side reimburses you for the cost of helping.</li>
</ul>

<h3><span class="clause">7.3</span> The ceiling on what anyone can owe</h3>
<p>Two separate limits, both written in capital letters because the law generally requires these to be conspicuous:</p>
<ul>
  <li><strong>No ripple-effect damages.</strong> Neither side can claim indirect losses — lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, destroyed data. Only direct, immediate harm counts. This holds even if the other side warned in advance that these losses could happen.</li>
  <li><strong>A total dollar cap.</strong> Everything either side could ever owe under this contract is capped at the higher of: the fees the customer paid (or owes) in the 12 months before the first thing went wrong, or $100,000. If 12 months of fees came to $40,000, the cap is $100,000. If they came to $250,000, the cap is $250,000.</li>
</ul>
<div class="exceptions">
  <p style="margin-bottom:.5rem"><strong>Four things break through both limits entirely:</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li>The indemnification promises in 7.1</li>
    <li>Leaking confidential information (covered in Section 9)</li>
    <li>Reckless carelessness or deliberate wrongdoing</li>
    <li>Stealing or infringing the other side's intellectual property</li>
  </ul>
</div>
<p style="margin-top:1rem">In those four situations there is no cap and no exclusion — liability is unlimited.</p>

<h2>Key Terms in Plain Language</h2>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr><th style="width:28%">Term</th><th>What it actually means</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td class="term">Indemnify</td><td>To cover someone else's costs when they get into legal trouble because of something you did. You pay so they don't have to.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Defend</td><td>Beyond just paying — you hire the lawyers and actually fight the lawsuit on their behalf.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Hold harmless</td><td>A promise that the other side won't end up financially worse off. Usually bundled with "indemnify" as belt-and-suspenders wording.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Indemnifying Party</td><td>The side doing the protecting and paying.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Indemnified Parties</td><td>The side being protected — here, the company plus its executives, board members, staff, and agents.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Third-party claim</td><td>A lawsuit or demand from someone outside the contract. This section does not cover the two parties suing each other.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Representation</td><td>A statement of fact you assert is true right now ("we own this code").</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Warranty</td><td>A guarantee about quality or performance, with a promise to make it right if it fails.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Covenant</td><td>A promise to do — or not do — something going forward.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Gross negligence</td><td>Far worse than an honest mistake. Reckless disregard for obvious risks.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Willful misconduct</td><td>Doing something you knew was wrong, on purpose.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Deliverables</td><td>The work products handed over under the contract — software, reports, designs, whatever was ordered.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Infringe</td><td>Using someone's patent, copyright, or trademark without permission.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Misappropriate</td><td>Taking or using someone's trade secret or confidential information improperly.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Materially prejudiced</td><td>Genuinely harmed in a way that matters — here, a late notice that actually hurt the defense, not one that was merely late.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Tender sole control</td><td>Hand over full authority to manage the lawsuit and decide on settlement.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Not to be unreasonably withheld</td><td>You have veto power, but you can't use it arbitrarily. You need a legitimate reason to say no.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Indirect / consequential damages</td><td>Knock-on losses that flow from the problem rather than being the problem itself — a factory idled because a delivered part failed.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Incidental damages</td><td>Small side costs of dealing with the problem, like shipping or inspection fees.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Special damages</td><td>Losses unique to your situation that wouldn't be obvious to an outsider.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Punitive / exemplary damages</td><td>Money awarded to punish bad behavior, over and above the actual loss.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Loss of goodwill</td><td>Damage to reputation and customer relationships.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Under any theory of liability</td><td>The limit applies no matter the legal label — breach of contract, negligence, or anything else.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Total cumulative liability</td><td>Everything added together across the life of the contract, not a fresh limit per incident.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="term">Fees paid or payable</td><td>Money already handed over plus money currently owed but not yet paid.</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h2>What to Watch For</h2>
<ul>
  <li><strong>The cap can be small.</strong> If the contract is low-value, $100,000 is the realistic ceiling on ordinary disputes — which may be far less than the harm a failure could cause.</li>
  <li><strong>"Lost profits" excluded is a big deal.</strong> For many business disputes, lost profits <em>are</em> the damage. Excluding them removes most of what you'd want to recover.</li>
  <li><strong>The carve-outs do the heavy lifting.</strong> The four exceptions in 7.3 are where real exposure lives. Whether a given dispute falls inside or outside them is often the whole fight.</li>
  <li><strong>Losing control of the defense has consequences.</strong> The other side picks the lawyers and the strategy. Your protection is limited to a veto on settlements that admit your fault or impose non-money obligations.</li>
  <li><strong>The IP exclusions can be broad in practice.</strong> Most delivered work gets modified or combined with other systems. Either can quietly void the IP protection.</li>
</ul>

<footer>
  This is a plain-language explanation of contract text, not legal advice. Specific wording, governing law, and the rest of the agreement can change how these provisions apply — consult a lawyer before relying on this summary.
</footer>

</div>

<h1>Section 7: Indemnification and Limitation of Liability</h1>
<p class="note">Plain-language summary and glossary</p>

<div class="task">
  <strong>Task:</strong> Summarize Section 7 of the contract for a non-technical reader and define the key legal terms in plain language.
</div>

<h2>The Bottom Line</h2>
<div class="bottom">
  Each side promises to cover the other's costs if an outsider sues over certain problems the first side caused. Separately, the contract caps how much either side can owe the other, and rules out "knock-on" damages like lost profits. Important exceptions apply to both the cap and the exclusion.
</div>

<h2>7.1 Each side protects the other from outside lawsuits</h2>
<p>If a <strong>third party</strong> (someone who isn't a party to this contract) makes a claim against one side, the other side may have to pay for the defense and any resulting costs. This applies when the claim comes from any of these:</p>
<ol>
  <li><strong>Breaking the contract:</strong> breaking a promise, guarantee, or obligation in the agreement.</li>
  <li><strong>Serious misconduct:</strong> extreme carelessness or intentional wrongdoing.</li>
  <li><strong>Intellectual property (IP) problems:</strong> a claim that the work delivered (the "Deliverables") copies or wrongly uses someone else's patents, copyrights, or similar rights.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Limits on the IP protection.</strong> It does not apply if the claim results from:</p>
<ul>
  <li>changes the other side made to the Deliverables,</li>
  <li>mixing the Deliverables with materials the delivering side didn't supply, where the problem wouldn't have happened without the mix, or</li>
  <li>using the Deliverables in a way the contract doesn't allow.</li>
</ul>
<p>Protection also extends to the other side's officers, directors, employees, and agents.</p>

<h2>7.2 How a claim must be handled</h2>
<p>The protected side must:</p>
<ol>
  <li><strong>Give prompt written notice.</strong> Late notice only hurts them if the delay seriously damaged the other side's ability to respond.</li>
  <li><strong>Let the paying side run the defense and any settlement.</strong> That side can't settle in a way that admits fault by the protected side, or forces them to do or stop doing something (other than pay money), without written permission. Permission can't be unreasonably refused.</li>
  <li><strong>Cooperate reasonably.</strong> The paying side covers the cost of that cooperation.</li>
</ol>

<h2>7.3 Limits on what either side can owe</h2>
<table>
  <tr><th>Rule</th><th>What it means</th></tr>
  <tr>
    <td><strong>No "knock-on" damages</strong></td>
    <td>Neither side can recover indirect losses, such as lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, lost data, or punitive (punishment) damages. This holds even if the other side was warned such losses were possible.</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td><strong>Dollar cap</strong></td>
    <td>Each side's total liability is capped at the <em>greater of</em>: (a) the fees paid or owed in the 12 months before the first triggering event, or (b) $100,000.</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td><strong>Exceptions</strong></td>
    <td>The exclusion above does <em>not</em> apply to: indemnification duties under 7.1, breaches of confidentiality (Section 9), gross negligence or willful misconduct, or one side infringing the other's IP.</td>
  </tr>
</table>
<p class="note"><strong>Worth noting:</strong> The wording says the dollar cap applies "subject to the foregoing," which is ambiguous. It may mean the cap also does not apply to the listed exceptions, or it may apply to everything. A lawyer should clarify this, since it decides whether those exceptions are uncapped.</p>

<h2>Key Terms in Plain Language</h2>
<dl>
  <dt>Indemnify</dt>
  <dd>To reimburse someone for losses or costs they suffer, typically from a lawsuit.</dd>

  <dt>Defend</dt>
  <dd>To take on the legal fight, and pay for it, when someone is sued.</dd>

  <dt>Hold harmless</dt>
  <dd>To promise the other side won't bear the financial hit from a covered problem.</dd>

  <dt>Indemnifying Party</dt>
  <dd>The side making the protection promise (each side plays this role for its own conduct).</dd>

  <dt>Indemnified Parties</dt>
  <dd>The side being protected, plus its officers, directors, employees, and agents.</dd>

  <dt>Third-party claim</dt>
  <dd>A complaint or lawsuit from someone outside the contract. It does not cover disputes between the two contracting sides.</dd>

  <dt>Losses</dt>
  <dd>The money at stake: damages, settlements, court judgments, fines, and reasonable legal fees.</dd>

  <dt>Representation, warranty, covenant</dt>
  <dd>Statements of fact (representation), guarantees (warranty), and promises to do or not do something (covenant) made in the contract.</dd>

  <dt>Gross negligence</dt>
  <dd>Extreme carelessness, well beyond an ordinary mistake.</dd>

  <dt>Willful misconduct</dt>
  <dd>Intentionally doing something wrong.</dd>

  <dt>Deliverables</dt>
  <dd>The products, work, or materials one side hands over to the other.</dd>

  <dt>Infringe / misappropriate</dt>
  <dd>To use someone's protected creation, invention, or trade secret without permission.</dd>

  <dt>Intellectual property (IP)</dt>
  <dd>Legally protected creations such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets.</dd>

  <dt>Tender control</dt>
  <dd>To hand over the running of the defense to the paying side.</dd>

  <dt>Materially prejudiced</dt>
  <dd>Seriously harmed in a meaningful way, for example because of a delayed notice.</dd>

  <dt>Indirect, incidental, consequential, special damages</dt>
  <dd>Losses that are side effects of a problem, not the direct result, such as a missed business deal caused by a late delivery.</dd>

  <dt>Punitive / exemplary damages</dt>
  <dd>Money awarded to punish wrongdoing, not to cover actual losses.</dd>

  <dt>Goodwill</dt>
  <dd>A business's reputation and customer relationships.</dd>

  <dt>Limitation of liability (cap)</dt>
  <dd>A ceiling on how much one side can be made to pay the other.</dd>
</dl>

<p class="note">This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Have a qualified attorney review the contract before relying on it.</p>

# Section 7 in Plain English: Who Pays When Something Goes Wrong

This section of the contract deals with two big questions: (1) if a third party sues one of the parties because of something the other party did, who has to defend the lawsuit and pay for it? And (2) if things really go sideways, what's the maximum amount either party could ever owe the other?

---

## 7.1 Mutual Indemnification — "You Broke It, You Handle It"

Both parties promise to protect each other from certain kinds of lawsuits brought by outsiders. If a third party (someone not part of this contract) sues one of the parties because of something the *other* party did wrong, the party at fault has to step in, hire lawyers, defend the case, and pay whatever the outcome costs — settlements, court judgments, fines, penalties, and legal fees.

This protection kicks in when the lawsuit is caused by:

- **(a)** The at-fault party breaking a promise it made in the contract (a "representation, warranty, or covenant").
- **(b)** The at-fault party being seriously careless ("gross negligence") or doing something intentionally harmful ("willful misconduct").
- **(c)** Someone claiming that the at-fault party's product or work ("Deliverables") copies or steals their intellectual property (like a patent, copyright, or trade secret).

**Important exceptions to (c):** The at-fault party does NOT have to cover the IP-infringement lawsuit if the problem was actually caused by the *other* side — specifically if the other side (i) modified the Deliverables themselves, (ii) combined the Deliverables with something else and the combination is what caused the infringement, or (iii) used the Deliverables in a way the contract didn't allow.

### Key terms defined:
- **Indemnify:** To financially protect someone — to cover their losses and legal costs.
- **Hold harmless:** Promise that the other side won't suffer any financial hit from the issue.
- **Third-party claim:** A lawsuit or demand from someone who isn't a party to this contract.
- **Deliverables:** The products, services, or work one party provides to the other under the contract.
- **Gross negligence:** A serious level of carelessness — much worse than a normal mistake.
- **Willful misconduct:** Doing something wrong on purpose, or with reckless disregard for the consequences.

---

## 7.2 Indemnification Procedure — The Rules of the Road

If a party wants the other side to defend and pay for a lawsuit under Section 7.1, they have to follow certain steps:

- **(a) Notify promptly, in writing.** The party being sued has to tell the other party about the lawsuit reasonably quickly. If they're late, they don't automatically lose their right to be defended — they only lose it to the extent that the delay actually hurt ("materially prejudiced") the other party's ability to defend.
- **(b) Hand over control of the defense.** The party paying for the defense gets to make the strategic calls — which lawyers to hire, whether to fight or settle. BUT: they can't agree to a settlement that admits the other side did something wrong, requires the other side to do something (beyond just paying money), or otherwise binds them, without first getting the other side's written OK. And the other side can't unreasonably refuse.
- **(c) Cooperate.** The party being defended has to help — hand over documents, make witnesses available, etc. — and the party paying for the defense covers the costs of that cooperation.

### Key terms defined:
- **Tender control of the defense:** Officially hand the lawsuit over so the other party runs the legal strategy.
- **Materially prejudiced:** Meaningfully harmed — not just technically inconvenienced.
- **Unreasonably withheld:** You can't say no just to be difficult; there has to be a real reason.

---

## 7.3 Limitation of Liability — The Financial Ceiling

This is the "even in the worst case, here's the most you can lose" clause. It has two parts.

### Part 1: No indirect damages
Neither party can sue the other for indirect or downstream financial harm — things like:
- **Lost profits** (money you would have made)
- **Lost revenue** (sales that didn't happen)
- **Loss of goodwill** (damage to reputation or brand value)
- **Loss of data**
- Or other "indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary" damages

This applies even if the party knew these losses were possible.

### Part 2: A dollar cap on everything else
For damages that ARE recoverable, each party's total combined liability under the contract is capped at the **greater of**:
- **(A)** The fees paid or owed under the contract during the 12 months before the incident that triggered the liability, OR
- **(B)** $100,000 USD

So if fees over the prior year were $60,000, the cap is $100,000. If fees were $500,000, the cap is $500,000. Whichever number is bigger wins.

### The big carve-outs (things NOT limited by this cap)
The protections above do NOT apply — meaning there's no dollar ceiling and indirect damages ARE on the table — for:
- **(i)** A party's indemnification duties under Section 7.1 (covering third-party lawsuits).
- **(ii)** Violations of confidentiality (Section 9 — leaking secrets).
- **(iii)** Gross negligence or willful misconduct.
- **(iv)** A party infringing the other party's own intellectual property.

For those four things, a party's exposure is potentially unlimited.

### Key terms defined:
- **Indirect / consequential damages:** Downstream losses that flow from the breach rather than being the breach itself — e.g., the customers you lost because your website went down.
- **Punitive / exemplary damages:** Money awarded by a court to punish bad behavior, over and above the actual harm.
- **Cumulative liability:** The total, added up across every claim under the contract — not per-incident.
- **Carve-out:** An exception to a general rule; here, situations where the liability cap doesn't apply.

---

## The Bottom Line

- If someone sues you because of something the other party did wrong, they'll defend you and pay the bill — as long as you tell them fast and let them run the defense.
- IP infringement is covered, unless *you* caused the problem by modifying or misusing what they gave you.
- In most disputes between the two parties, neither side can go after "lost profits" or similar downstream losses, and total damages are capped (at the greater of the last year's fees or $100,000).
- But that cap and those protections disappear for the really serious stuff: indemnification obligations, leaking confidential info, gross negligence, willful misconduct, and stealing the other party's IP. For those, the sky is the limit.

# Plain-Language Summary of Section 7 (Indemnification and Limitation of Liability)

## What This Section Does

This section covers two things: (1) when one party has to cover the other party's losses from lawsuits or claims brought by outsiders, and (2) a cap on how much either party can be forced to pay if something goes wrong.

## Key Terms, Defined

- **Indemnify / Hold Harmless**: To cover someone else's losses and legal costs so they don't have to pay out of pocket.
- **Indemnifying Party**: The party who has agreed to cover the other side's losses in a given situation.
- **Indemnified Parties**: The party (and its officers, directors, employees, and agents) who receive that protection.
- **Claims**: Lawsuits, demands, or legal proceedings brought by a third party (someone outside this contract).
- **Losses**: The money that results from a Claim — damages, settlements, fines, and legal fees.
- **Deliverables**: The product, software, or work being provided under the contract.
- **Gross Negligence / Willful Misconduct**: Behavior far worse than an honest mistake — either reckless disregard for consequences or intentional wrongdoing.
- **Intellectual Property (IP)**: Legally protected creations like patents, copyrights, and trade secrets.

## 7.1 — Mutual Indemnification

Either party can be required to cover the other party's losses from a third-party lawsuit, but only in specific situations:

1. The party broke a promise it made in the contract.
2. The party acted with gross negligence or intentional misconduct.
3. The party's deliverables (when used as intended under the contract) allegedly steal or infringe someone else's intellectual property.

**Important carve-out on #3**: If the IP claim actually comes from the other party changing the deliverables, mixing them with something else that caused the problem, or using them in a way the contract didn't allow, then the providing party is off the hook — the party who caused the misuse bears responsibility instead.

**In plain terms**: If you break your promises, act recklessly, or your product infringes someone's IP (through no fault of the other party's own misuse), you have to cover the other side's legal losses from any resulting lawsuit.

## 7.2 — Indemnification Procedure

If a party wants to be covered for a claim, it must:

1. **Tell the other party quickly, in writing**, once it learns of the claim. (Being late doesn't fully cancel the protection — only if the delay actually hurt the other party's ability to defend the case.)
2. **Let the covering party run the defense** — meaning the party paying for the defense also controls the legal strategy and any settlement. However, that party can't settle in a way that admits wrongdoing, forces the other party to do something (beyond paying money), or binds the other party — without the other party's okay (which can't be refused for no good reason).
3. **Cooperate reasonably** with the defense, with expenses reimbursed.

**In plain terms**: Speak up fast if you're sued, hand the steering wheel to whoever is paying for your defense, and help out when asked — they'll cover reasonable costs of your cooperation.

## 7.3 — Limitation of Liability

This part sets a ceiling on how much money either party can ever be forced to pay the other, with some exceptions.

**Exceptions (no dollar cap applies to these)**:
- Indemnification obligations from 7.1 (above)
- Breaches of confidentiality
- Gross negligence or willful misconduct
- Infringing the other party's intellectual property

**For everything else**:
- **Neither party owes the other for indirect or knock-on damages** — things like lost profits, lost revenue, lost business reputation, or lost data — even if it was told those losses were possible. Only direct losses are on the table.
- **There's a total dollar cap** on liability for everything else. It's whichever is greater:
  - (a) The fees paid (or owed) under the contract in the 12 months before the incident that caused the problem, or
  - (b) $100,000.

**In plain terms**: For most disputes, the most either side can be forced to pay is capped at either what was paid in fees over the past year or $100,000 — whichever is more — and neither side has to pay for indirect losses like lost profits. But that cap doesn't apply to the big stuff: violating confidentiality, IP infringement, reckless/intentional misconduct, or the indemnification duties described in 7.1. Those risks are open-ended.

# Section 7 in Plain Language — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

This section answers two questions: (1) if an outsider sues one party because of something the other party did, who pays? and (2) if the two parties end up in a dispute with each other, how much money can be at stake?

## 7.1 — Mutual Indemnification ("you break it, you cover it")

Each party promises to protect the other from lawsuits brought by outside third parties, but only when the lawsuit is caused by one of three things:

1. **A broken promise.** The party breached a representation, warranty, or covenant it made in the agreement.
2. **Serious misconduct.** The party was grossly negligent or acted with willful misconduct (not ordinary carelessness; see definitions below).
3. **An IP infringement claim.** Someone claims the party's Deliverables, when used as the agreement allows, infringe or misappropriate their intellectual property.

The protection covers the other party plus its officers, directors, employees, and agents. It covers essentially every kind of cost: damages, settlements, judgments, fines, penalties, and reasonable outside lawyer fees.

**Exceptions to the IP protection.** The IP indemnity does not apply if the infringement claim happens because the protected party:
- modified the Deliverables itself,
- combined the Deliverables with materials the indemnifying party did not supply (and the combination is what infringes), or
- used the Deliverables outside the scope the agreement expressly permits.

In short: the party that created the problem pays for it, unless the other party caused the IP problem by tinkering with, combining, or misusing the Deliverables.

## 7.2 — Indemnification Procedure (how to actually claim the protection)

If a party wants the other side to cover a third-party claim, it has to follow three steps:

1. **Notify promptly, in writing.** Being late does not automatically forfeit the protection; the indemnifying party is excused only to the extent the delay actually hurt its position ("materially prejudiced").
2. **Hand over control of the defense and settlement.** The indemnifying party runs the case and decides whether to settle. One limit: it cannot agree to a settlement that admits liability on the protected party's behalf or imposes non-monetary obligations on the protected party without that party's written consent, and that consent cannot be unreasonably withheld.
3. **Cooperate reasonably**, with the indemnifying party paying the costs of that cooperation.

## 7.3 — Limitation of Liability (the cap on what either party can owe the other)

This clause limits how much either party can be held responsible for in a dispute between the two of them. It has two parts:

**Part 1: No indirect damages.** Neither party is liable to the other for indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages, or for lost profits, lost revenue, loss of goodwill, or loss of data. This applies regardless of the legal theory used and even if the party was warned such losses could happen.

**Part 2: Dollar cap.** Beyond that, each party's total liability under the agreement is capped at the greater of:
- (A) the fees paid or payable by the Customer to the Provider in the 12 months before the first event that triggered the liability, or
- (B) $100,000.

**Carve-outs (the cap and the indirect-damages exclusion do not apply to these):**
- indemnification obligations under 7.1,
- breaches of confidentiality under Section 9,
- gross negligence or willful misconduct,
- infringement of the other party's intellectual property rights.

For those four categories, liability is unlimited.

## Key Terms Defined

- **Indemnify / hold harmless** — To take on financial responsibility for someone else's losses. If you indemnify me, you pay the costs of a claim against me that is your fault.
- **Defend** — To handle and pay for the legal defense of a lawsuit on someone's behalf.
- **Indemnifying Party** — The party paying and protecting. **Indemnified Parties** — The party being protected, plus its officers, directors, employees, and agents.
- **Third-party claim** — A claim by someone who is not a party to this contract (a customer, a competitor, a regulator, etc.). Indemnification is about outside claims, not disputes between the two contracting parties.
- **Claims / Losses** — Defined catch-all terms. "Claims" is any demand, lawsuit, or proceeding; "Losses" is every kind of cost that flows from it, including reasonable outside lawyer fees.
- **Representation, warranty, covenant** — Three types of contractual promises: a representation is a statement of fact, a warranty is a guarantee that something is or will be true, and a covenant is a promise to do (or not do) something.
- **Gross negligence** — Extreme carelessness, well beyond an ordinary mistake; a reckless disregard for obvious risks.
- **Willful misconduct** — Intentional wrongdoing, or knowingly acting in a way that is wrong.
- **Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property** — Using someone's patent, copyright, or trademark without permission (infringe) or wrongfully taking their trade secrets (misappropriate).
- **Deliverables** — The work product delivered under the agreement (defined elsewhere in the contract).
- **Materially prejudiced** — Actually harmed in a meaningful way, for example if late notice meant a defense deadline was missed.
- **Tender control of the defense** — Hand the lawsuit over to the other party's lawyers to manage.
- **Consent not unreasonably withheld** — You can say no to a settlement, but only for a legitimate reason.
- **Direct damages** — Losses that flow immediately and obviously from a breach (e.g., the cost of fixing or replacing what was promised).
- **Indirect / consequential damages** — Downstream losses that result from a breach but are one step removed, such as lost business, lost profits, or reputational harm.
- **Incidental damages** — Smaller costs incurred while dealing with a breach, like expenses to find a replacement.
- **Special damages** — Losses specific to a party's particular situation rather than what anyone would suffer.
- **Punitive / exemplary damages** — Extra money a court awards to punish egregious conduct, not to compensate for a loss.
- **Goodwill** — The value of a business's reputation and customer relationships.
- **Theory of liability** — The legal basis for a claim (breach of contract, negligence, etc.). The exclusion applies no matter which one is used.
- **Cumulative liability** — All liability added together across the whole life of the agreement, not per incident.
- **Fees paid or payable** — Amounts the Customer has already paid plus amounts it owes but has not yet paid.

## Bottom Line

- If an outsider sues because of your breach, your serious misconduct, or your infringing work product, you pay, provided the other side notifies you, lets you run the defense, and cooperates.
- Between the two parties, each can only be liable for direct losses, capped at the higher of the last 12 months of fees or $100,000.
- The cap disappears entirely for indemnification, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence or willful misconduct, and IP infringement.

This is a summary for general understanding, not legal advice; a lawyer should review the full agreement before you rely on it.

**Plain-English summary:** Section 7 says each side must protect the other from certain outside claims they cause, follow a set process if a claim happens, and accept tight limits on most kinds of damages.

**7.1 Mutual indemnification:** If one party causes certain legal problems, that party must step in and cover the other side’s losses. This applies if the problem comes from:
1. breaking promises or obligations in the contract,
2. serious carelessness or intentional bad acts, or
3. claims that its deliverables violate someone else’s intellectual property rights.

But the IP protection does **not** apply if the other side changed the deliverables, combined them with other materials in a way that caused the problem, or used them outside the contract’s allowed scope.

**7.2 Claim procedure:** The protected party must notify the other side promptly in writing, let that other side control the defense and settlement, and reasonably cooperate. But the defending party cannot settle in a way that admits fault for the protected party or puts non-money obligations on them unless they agree in writing.

**7.3 Liability limits:** In most cases, neither side can recover indirect or hard-to-measure damages like lost profits, lost revenue, lost data, lost goodwill, or punitive damages. There are important exceptions: these limits do **not** apply to indemnification duties, confidentiality breaches, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or one party infringing the other party’s IP rights. For claims where the cap does apply, the most either side can owe is the higher of:
1. the fees paid or owed in the prior 12 months, or
2. **$100,000**.

**Key legal terms in plain language:**

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Reimburse or cover the other side’s losses. |
| **Defend** | Handle the legal defense, usually by managing lawyers and the case. |
| **Hold harmless** | Protect the other side from having to bear the cost or liability. |
| **Indemnifying Party** | The side that must protect and pay if a covered claim happens. |
| **Indemnified Parties** | The side being protected, plus its people like officers, employees, and agents. |
| **Third-party claim** | A claim brought by someone outside the contract, not one of the two parties. |
| **Representation / warranty / covenant** | A statement of fact, a promise something is true or will work a certain way, or a contractual promise to do or not do something. |
| **Gross negligence** | More than ordinary carelessness; very serious neglect. |
| **Willful misconduct** | Intentional wrongful behavior. |
| **Deliverables** | The products, work, software, services, or materials one party is supposed to provide. |
| **Infringe / misappropriate intellectual property rights** | Use someone else’s protected invention, code, content, trademark, or trade secret without the legal right to do so. |
| **Settle / settlement** | Resolve a claim without finishing the full court process. |
| **Non-monetary obligation** | Something you must do other than pay money, like admit fault, stop using something, or change business practices. |
| **Indirect / consequential / special / punitive damages** | Losses that are not direct out-of-pocket harm, or damages meant to punish; these are usually harder to recover. |
| **Lost goodwill** | Harm to reputation or customer trust. |
| **Cumulative liability** | The total amount a party can owe under the contract overall. |
| **Fees paid or payable** | Money already paid, plus amounts that are due under the contract. |

**Bottom line:** Each side covers the other for serious problems it causes, especially contract breaches, misconduct, and some IP claims. But outside those carve-outs, both sides sharply limit what kinds of damages can be claimed and cap total exposure.

## Bottom line

Section 7 says two things: **each side cleans up the legal messes it causes**, and **neither side can be sued for unlimited amounts** — with a few big exceptions.

---

## 7.1 — Mutual Indemnification ("I'll cover you if I cause the problem")

If a third party (someone outside this contract) sues one of you, the party *at fault* pays for the defense and the damages. This works both ways.

You cover the other side when the lawsuit comes from:
- **(a)** You broke a promise in this contract
- **(b)** You were extremely careless or did something deliberately wrong
- **(c)** Someone claims your work product (the "Deliverables") steals their intellectual property

**Three carve-outs to (c)** — you're *off the hook* for IP claims if the problem came from:
1. The other side modified your work
2. The other side combined your work with something you didn't supply, and *that combination* caused the infringement
3. The other side used your work in a way the contract never allowed

## 7.2 — How the process works

1. **Tell them fast.** If you get sued, notify the other party in writing. Being slow doesn't void their obligation — unless the delay actually damaged their ability to defend.
2. **Hand over the wheel.** The party paying gets to run the defense and decide settlement terms. *But* they can't sign a settlement that admits you did something wrong, or makes you do something non-monetary, without your written OK.
3. **Help out.** You cooperate; they pay your costs for cooperating.

## 7.3 — Limitation of Liability (the damage cap)

**Two separate limits, both in ALL CAPS because they matter:**

**Limit 1 — No indirect damages.** Neither side can claim lost profits, lost revenue, reputational harm, or lost data. Only direct, immediate losses count.

**Limit 2 — A dollar ceiling.** Total liability is capped at whichever is *bigger*:
- Fees paid in the 12 months before the problem started, **or**
- $100,000

**Four exceptions where neither limit applies** (unlimited exposure):
1. Indemnification duties from 7.1
2. Breaking confidentiality (Section 9)
3. Gross negligence or willful misconduct
4. Infringing the other party's IP

---

## Key terms, plain language

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Pay the other side's legal bills and losses |
| **Hold harmless** | Make sure they don't end up out of pocket |
| **Third-party claim** | A lawsuit from an outsider, not from each other |
| **Gross negligence** | Not just a mistake — recklessly careless |
| **Willful misconduct** | You knew it was wrong and did it anyway |
| **Misappropriate** | Take someone's trade secret or IP without permission |
| **Consequential damages** | Knock-on losses (a factory sits idle because your software failed) |
| **Punitive damages** | Extra money awarded to punish, not to repay |
| **Materially prejudiced** | The delay genuinely hurt their case |
| **Not unreasonably withheld** | You can say no, but you need a real reason |
| **Cumulative liability** | Everything added together across the whole contract, not per incident |

---

## What to watch

- **The cap is "greater of," which favors you on small contracts.** On a $30k/year deal, your floor is still $100k.
- **The exceptions in 7.3 swallow a lot.** Indemnification obligations are uncapped — so an IP lawsuit could exceed the cap by a wide margin.
- **Giving up defense control (7.2b) is standard but real.** The other side picks the lawyers and the strategy for a case with your name on it.

# Section 7 Summary: Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

Your text had missing words, so I filled gaps from standard contract language. I flag the one place where the gap changes the meaning.

## In short
Each side promises to cover the other's costs if a third party sues over certain problems the first side caused. The section also sets rules for how that works. Finally, it limits how much either side can owe the other, with some exceptions.

## 7.1 Mutual Indemnification (each side protects the other)
**What it says:** Each party (the "Indemnifying Party") must defend the other party and its officers, directors, employees, and agents (the "Indemnified Parties"). It must also cover their costs when an outsider brings a claim arising from any of these:
- **(a)** The indemnifying party broke a promise, guarantee, or obligation in the contract.
- **(b)** The indemnifying party was grossly negligent or acted intentionally wrong.
- **(c)** The indemnifying party's deliverables (the work product it provides), used as the contract allows, are alleged to infringe someone else's intellectual property.

**Exclusions for (c):** The IP protection likely does *not* apply if the claim comes from:
1. Changes the protected party made to the deliverables.
2. Combining the deliverables with materials the indemnifying party didn't supply, where the combination caused the infringement.
3. Using the deliverables in a way the contract doesn't permit.

## 7.2 Procedure (what the protected party must do)
1. **Give prompt written notice** of the claim. Late notice doesn't cancel the other side's duty, unless the delay materially harmed them.
2. **Hand over control** of the defense and settlement to the indemnifying party. That party can't settle in a way that admits fault for, or imposes non-money obligations on, the protected party without written consent. Consent can't be unreasonably refused.
3. **Cooperate reasonably**, at the indemnifying party's expense.

## 7.3 Limitation of Liability (caps on what you can owe)
**Two limits apply:**
- **No "indirect" damages.** Neither party owes the other indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages. That includes lost profits, lost revenue, lost goodwill, and lost data. This holds even if they were warned such damages were possible.
- **A dollar cap.** Each party's total liability under the whole agreement can't exceed the **greater of**:
  - (A) the fees paid or payable in the 12 months before the first event that caused liability, or
  - (B) **$100,000**.

**Exceptions to the damages exclusion:** These four items are carved out:
1. Indemnification obligations under 7.1.
2. Breaches of confidentiality (Section 9).
3. Gross negligence or willful misconduct.
4. Infringing the other party's intellectual property.

**Caution:** The cap begins "subject to the foregoing," which is ambiguous. It could mean the four exceptions are also *uncapped*, or that they're exempt only from the damages exclusion and still capped. That difference could be worth a lot of money, so check the original wording and consider asking counsel.

## Key terms in plain language

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| **Indemnify** | Reimburse someone for losses they suffer |
| **Defend** | Handle and pay for the legal fight |
| **Hold harmless** | Don't make the other party bear the loss |
| **Third-party claim** | A lawsuit or demand from someone outside the contract |
| **Losses** | Money costs: damages, settlements, fines, and reasonable lawyer fees |

| **Representation / warranty / covenant** | A statement of fact / a guarantee / a promise to do or not do something |

| **Willful misconduct** | Deliberately doing something wrong |
| **Deliverables** | The work or products one party provides to the other |
| **Misappropriate** | Wrongfully use someone else's protected information or ideas |
| **Intellectual property** | Patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets |
| **Indirect / consequential damages** | Knock-on losses, not the direct cost of the breach (such as lost business from an outage) |
| **Punitive / exemplary damages** | Extra money meant to punish, not compensate |
| **Goodwill** | A business's reputation and customer relationships |
| **Cumulative liability** | The total owed across all claims combined |

- Hold harmless = shield from loss.
- Deliverables = things provided under contract.
- Gross negligence = extreme carelessness.
- Willful misconduct = intentional wrongdoing.
- Consequential/indirect damages = downstream losses (lost profits, lost revenue).
- Cap / limitation of liability = ceiling on total money owed.

# Q3 Planning — Product / Engineering / Ops sync — 2026-08-27

**Attendees:** Priya (PM), Marcus (Eng lead), Jenna (Ops), Dan (Design), Sara (VP Product)

---

**Priya:** Thanks all for joining. Big agenda — we need to lock Q3 scope by Friday, then Sara can take it to the exec review Monday. Three headliners on the table: the reconciliation revamp, the mobile receipt-capture feature, and the vendor payout SLA push. Let's start with reconciliation.

**Marcus:** So on reconciliation — the current engine chokes on multi-currency batches. We've had three incidents this quarter and support ticket volume for reconciliation issues is up 40% quarter over quarter. My team scoped a rewrite that's roughly six engineer-weeks. That includes migrating the FX rounding module. We'd need Karim from platform for two of those weeks to help with the ledger integration.

**Sara:** Six engineer-weeks is a lot. What's the buy-vs-build here? Is there a vendor?

**Marcus:** We looked at two — Recur and LedgerFlow. Recur is $180K/year for our volume, LedgerFlow is $140K but doesn't handle our jurisdiction-specific tax codes. Both would still need integration work, probably three engineer-weeks. Not a great deal.

**Sara:** Okay, build wins. Priya, put reconciliation as the Q3 anchor. Marcus, sync with Karim's manager this week and confirm his availability.

**Priya:** Noted. Mobile receipt-capture next. Dan, where are we on design?

**Dan:** Flows are done, prototype tested with six users. Two big things came out of testing: users want to bulk-select receipts before uploading, and the OCR confidence indicator needs to be way more prominent. Bulk-select is not currently in scope; that would add maybe a sprint of work.

**Marcus:** If bulk-select is a sprint I'd want to descope something else. We're already stretched with reconciliation.

**Sara:** Let's ship v1 without bulk-select. Add a note to the roadmap for a fast-follow. Dan, please update the specs.

**Dan:** Will do by Wednesday.

**Priya:** Vendor payout SLA — Jenna, this one's yours.

**Jenna:** Right. The finance team wants us to guarantee payouts within 48 hours from invoice approval. Current p95 is 71 hours. Two bottlenecks: manual approval routing (that's ops), and the batching window on the ACH send job (that's eng). If eng cuts the batching window from 12 hours to 4, and ops adds a second approver on the west-coast shift, we can hit 48h p95 by mid-Q3.

**Marcus:** Cutting the ACH batch window means more ACH files per day, more monitoring overhead. Doable but not free — half a sprint of eng time plus SRE sign-off.

**Sara:** Do the trade-off analysis and bring it back next week. If SRE says the monitoring load is manageable, we do it. Otherwise we look at intermediate targets.

**Priya:** Two smaller things — the audit-log retention update is being pushed to Q4, that's confirmed with Legal. And the internal admin-tool refresh is still owned by the intern crew, no changes there.

**Sara:** One last thing. HR flagged that we've had a spike in bug-bash burnout on the engineering side. Marcus, can you propose a rotating on-call structure by end of month? Doesn't need to be big, just a proposal.

**Marcus:** Yep, I'll have something by the 31st.

**Priya:** Okay. Recap next steps then. Marcus: confirm Karim, propose on-call rotation by 31st, do ACH trade-off analysis. Dan: update mobile specs by Wednesday. Jenna: pair with Marcus on the ACH analysis. Sara: exec review Monday. I'll circulate the scope draft Thursday morning for review before Friday lock.

**Sara:** Good. Thanks everyone.

## Key Decisions & Points

### Reconciliation Revamp (Q3 Anchor)

- Requires Karim from platform for 2 weeks (ledger integration)

### Mobile Receipt-Capture
- Design flows done; prototype tested with 6 users
- User testing surfaced two needs: bulk-select before upload, and more prominent OCR confidence indicator
- Bulk-select would add ~1 sprint — descoped from v1
- **Decision:** Ship v1 without bulk-select; add bulk-select as a fast-follow on the roadmap

### Vendor Payout SLA
- Finance wants 48-hour payout guarantee from invoice approval; current p95 is 71 hours
- Two bottlenecks: manual approval routing (ops) and 12-hour ACH batching window (eng)
- Proposal: cut ACH batching window from 12h to 4h + add west-coast shift second approver → 48h p95 by mid-Q3
- ACH change costs ~half a sprint of eng time plus SRE sign-off (more ACH files/day, more monitoring overhead)
- **Decision:** Pending trade-off analysis next week; proceed if SRE says monitoring load is manageable, otherwise consider intermediate targets

### Other Items
- Audit-log retention update pushed to Q4 (confirmed with Legal)
- Internal admin-tool refresh stays with the intern crew — no changes
- HR flagged bug-bash burnout on engineering; a rotating on-call proposal is needed
